title: Generation of new cisgenic apple lines resistant to either apple scab or fire blight
text:
Communicated by Stefan de Folter.
Cisgenic introduction of Rvi15 or FB_MR5 into ‘Gala’ generated single-copy lines with ≤ 201 bp vector remnants and high disease resistance, supporting cisgenesis as a powerful tool for commercial apple improvement.
Cisgenesis can be used to transfer disease resistance genes from wild apple germplasm into established apple cultivars, reducing their susceptibility to diseases. This approach allows combining disease resistance and fruit quality traits without compromising the desirable characteristics of the original cultivar. In our study, we used the binary plasmid vector pMF1 to create three apple scab-resistant cisgenic ‘Gala’ lines with the apple scab resistance gene Rvi15 , and three fire blight-resistant cisgenic 'Gala' lines with the fire blight resistance gene FB_MR5 . Quantitative PCR revealed that five of six cisgenic lines had a single integrated T-DNA copy, and targeted locus amplification enabled the identification and characterization of insertion sites in five lines. All characterized lines showed T-DNA trimming at the borders, with a total length of non-endogenous sequences at their respective insertion sites ranging from 135 to 201 base pairs. The presence of such residual vector sequences can influence the regulatory status of cisgenic plants, as some countries may classify these lines as genetically modified plants. All cisgenic lines exhibited increased disease resistance compared to the untransformed control genotype ‘Gala’. However, the achieved resistances are based on single genes, and it will be necessary to develop combinations of different resistance genes for more durable resistance. Resistance, durability, and evolving regulatory frameworks are crucial factors that together will determine the success of the cisgenic approach in achieving both high fruit quality and resistance for sustainable apple production.

Apple ( Malus domestica Borkh.) production is threatened by several diseases. While chemical control is effective against fungal pathogens, e.g., Venturia inaequalis it can be ineffective against Erwinia amylovora , the bacterial pathogen causing fire blight. The most sustainable approach to reducing crop losses and chemical inputs is the use of disease-resistant cultivars. However, most commercially successful apple cultivars are susceptible to diseases, and introgressing major disease resistance genes from wild apple genotypes requires time and extensive breeding efforts (Schlathölter et al. 2018 ) and will always lead to the development of novel cultivars with new characteristics.
Cisgenesis enables increasing disease resistance in an established cultivar without compromising its desirable characteristics. This is achieved using genetic modification techniques to amend established cultivars with resistance genes (including their native regulatory sequences) from sexually compatible donors (Schouten et al. 2006 ). Cisgenesis in apple was achieved by Agrobacterium -mediated plant transformation using either binary vectors pMF1 (Schaart et al. 2004 ) or p9-Dao-FLPi (Würdig et al. 2015 ). These vectors carry different inducible recombinase systems, allowing the excision of non-endogenous sequences required for the generation process (e.g., antibiotic resistance for selection) but unwanted in the final product. Most transgenic or vector-derived sequences are removed when the recombination system is activated in a transgenic intermediate line. However, recombination often leaves some non-endogenous sequences in the final product, including the left and right T-DNA borders, a recombinase recognition site, and spacer sequences used for cloning. The length of integrated non-endogenous sequences after recombination is expected to be greater for vector p9-Dao-FLPi than for pMF1. When cloning the fire blight resistance gene FB_MR5 from the wild apple Malus x robusta 5 into both vectors, the non-endogenous sequence between the left border (LB) and FB_MR5 is approximately 420 bp in p9-Dao-FLPi and 169 bp in pMF1. At the right border (RB), these lengths are 116 bp and 60 bp, respectively (Kost et al. 2015 ; Schaart et al. 2004 ; Würdig et al. 2015 ). Despite this, the extent of non-endogenous sequences in the final cisgenic line can vary; it can be larger or smaller than expected. It may be larger, because vector-derived sequences flanking the T-DNA could also be unexpectedly integrated due to a leaky T-DNA LB, leading in some cases to the incorrect excision of the T-DNA and resulting in the integration of part of the transformation plasmid backbone, as observed using both vectors (Kost et al. 2015 ; Vanblaere et al. 2014 ). It may be smaller because T-DNA extremities can be trimmed during integration, resulting in T-DNA RB and/or LB truncation or absence at insertion sites (Dalla Costa et al. 2020 ). The extent of non-endogenous sequences detectable in the final product could become a decisive criterion if future regulatory frameworks differentiate categories of genetically modified (GM) plants, regardless of the biosafety risks associated with such sequences.
The cisgenic approach improved the resistance of the cultivar ‘Gala’ against the most problematic diseases in apple orchards. Resistance to apple scab was conferred by Rvi6 (Joshi et al. 2011 ; Krens et al. 2015 ; Vanblaere et al. 2011 , 2014 ; Würdig et al. 2015 ), while fire blight resistance was conferred by FB_MR5 (Kost et al. 2015 ). This latter cisgenic line C44.4.146 was investigated in a field trial over 5 years (Schlathölter et al. 2021 , 2022 , 2023 ). The described cisgenic lines were generated for research, not commercial release or apple production. Neither resistance gene is durable in the field, as shown by the reported emergence of pathogen strains able to overcome these major resistance genes (Parisi et al. 1993 ; Vogt et al. 2013 ). While no other fire blight resistance genes have been cloned and validated, the apple scab resistance genes Rvi15 from GMAL2473 (Schouten et al. 2014 ) and Rvi12 Hansen’s baccata #2 (Yousaf et al. 2025 ) were cloned. No virulent strains were able to grow on GMAL2473, the differential host used to monitor Rvi15 , while rare events of resistance breakdown to Rvi12 were observed within the international monitoring project on apple scab virulence VINQUEST (Patocchi et al. 2020 ). However, Peil et al. ( 2023 ) showed that Rvi4 and Rvi15 are the same gene, and virulent strains have already been reported for Rvi4 (category “sometimes overcome”, Patocchi et al. 2020 ).
This work aims to generate FB_MR5 fire blight or Rvi15 apple scab-resistant cisgenic apple lines using the pMF1 vector and their functional and molecular characterization. The molecular analysis focuses on the characterization of the insertion sites, the extent of non-endogenous sequences at T-DNA-genome junctions, and the consistency of the recombinase-based excision system of the pMF1 vector.
The binary vector pMF1:: FB_MR5 was purchased from DNA Cloning Service e.K. (Hamburg, DE). It was obtained by cloning the FB_MR5 resistance gene with 1995 bp of 5’-UTR and 1,547 bp of 3’-UTR into the vector pMF1 (Suppl. Fig. S1 ).
The in vitro ‘Gala Galaxy’ apple line, kindly provided by Dr. Elisabeth Chevreau (INRAe, Angers, FR), and previously used for generating the cisgenic line C44.4.146 (Kost et al. 2015 ; Schlathölter et al. 2023 ), was used for transformation. In vitro cultures of the transgenic apple lines 603 and 604, generated using the pMF1:: Rvi15 ( Vr2-C ) vector for transformation of a different in vitro ‘Gala’ line (Schouten et al. 2014 ), were also used. Additionally, transgenic lines 605 and 606, generated but not reported in the same study, were provided and included in this work. For clarity, a "t” or a “c” was added in front of the transgenic event number (e.g., t603) to distinguish them from the derived cisgenic lines, respectively.
Plant transformation using the pMF1:: FB_MR5 binary vector was performed as described by Vanblaere et al. ( 2011 ). DNA was extracted from leaves of regenerated transgenic plantlets and tested by PCR to confirm the presence of the T-DNA and absence of vector backbone sequences using primers IPCR_codA_1 and pmf_bb2 (Vanblaere et al. 2014 ). The cisgenic lines were regenerated from intermediate transgenic lines (carrying FB_MR5 or Rvi15 ), following induction of the recombinase-R by dexamethasone treatment as described by Vanblaere et al. ( 2011 ), causing an excision of the unwanted transgenic sequences. Regenerants were maintained on elongation medium and tested for the absence of the gene NptII , present on the excisable transgenic cassette, as described by Vanblaere et al. ( 2011 ). From each transgenic line, a single cisgenic plant was regenerated and investigated, except for t603, where five independent cisgenic regenerants (cisgenic sublines c603.1-c603.5) were used to investigate the consistency of the recombination process. For all other analyses, only the first regenerant (c603.1, referred to as c603) was considered. Cisgenic lines were acclimatized to greenhouse conditions by micrografting onto apple seedlings (Joshi et al. 2011 ), grown to a shoot length of approximately 1 m, and multiplied by grafting on M9 T337 rootstocks to produce the replicates necessary for the disease resistance tests and further molecular characterization.
Two-to-three single leaves were collected from plants grown in the greenhouse for each investigated genotype and freeze-dried. The plant tissue was mechanically homogenized with glass beads using a Savant Bio 101 FastPrep cell homogenizer (Savant, Holbrook, NY, USA). DNA was extracted using the DNeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen, Düsseldorf, Germany) and quantified on a Nanodrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, USA).
The copy number of the resistance gene integration events in the cisgenic lines was determined by qPCR using specific TaqMan assays for each resistance gene. The elongation factor gene EF1α served as a reference gene (Gusberti et al. 2012 ). The assay developed by Kost et al. ( 2015 ) was used for FB_MR5 . A new TaqMan assay was developed for Rvi15 , using the primers Rvi15q1 forward and reverse (each at a final concentration of 900 nM), and the Rvi15 TaqMan probe at a final concentration of 250 nM. Primer and probe sequences are provided in Suppl. Table S1 . The qPCR mix contained 3 µl DNA in a 10 µl reaction with TaqMan Fast Universal Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, USA). The reaction was performed on a 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR system (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, USA) using the following conditions: 20 s at 95 °C, followed by 40 cycles of 3 s at 95 °C and 60 s at 60 °C. DNA of the cisgenic line C44.4.146, known to carry a single copy of FB_MR5 (Kost et al. 2015 ), and GMAL2473 ( Rvi15 donor) were used as positive controls. DNA from 'Gala' served as negative control. Each sample was investigated in triplicate. Ratios were calculated from the Ct values following the assessment of target-specific efficiency using a dilution series (1:10) in triplicate, applying the formula for relative quantification (Pfaffl 2001 ).
The insertion sites were determined by targeted locus amplification (TLA) technology. High-molecular-weight DNA of the cisgenic lines was extracted according to the protocol “Preparing Arabidopsis Genomic DNA for Size-Selected ~ 20 kb SMRTbell ™ Libraries (PacBio SampleNet)”, pooled, and delivered to Cergentis (now Solvia NL, Utrecht, The Netherlands). TLA analysis was performed using primers specifically binding to portions of the T-DNA after excision (Suppl. Table S2 ). Sequences flanking the insertion sites were provided by Cergentis and mapped to the apple genome GDDH13 (Daccord et al. 2017 ) to identify the location of the insertion site in the genome. The genomic sequences flanking the insertion site were used to design specific primers (Suppl. Table S3 ), which were combined with primers on the T-DNA for PCR amplification of the T-DNA-genome junctions from DNA extracted from young apple leaves as described above. PCR was performed using the HotStarTaq PCR kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) following the manufacturer’s protocol, in a 10 µl reaction with 2 µl DNA and an annealing temperature of 58 °C. PCR products were separated on a 1% agarose gel (80 V, 40 min) and visualized with ethidium bromide to confirm successful amplification. Amplicons were subsequently purified using the Multiscreen PCR 96 purification plate (Millipore, Burlington, USA), and Sanger sequenced (ABI 3130xl sequencer, Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, USA). Sequences were aligned and compared to the expected T-DNA structure and the genomic sequences at the insertion in the untransformed background ‘Gala Galaxy’.
Three independent inoculation experiments were performed using 8–12 grafted plantlets of the cisgenic lines c47, c49, and c53, and ‘Gala Galaxy’ as susceptible control, grafted on M9 T337 rootstocks. Prior to inoculation, plantlets were grown for 4–6 weeks in the greenhouse until they reached the 6–8 leaf stages. Inoculations followed the protocol of Peil et al. ( 2007 ): the two youngest leaves of each plantlet were cut with scissors that had been dipped in a suspension of E. amylovora strain EA222_JKI at a concentration of approximately 2 billion bacteria per milliliter (OD 600nm = 1.03–1.05 in phosphate-buffered saline, PBS). The percentage of lesion length was recorded 21 days post-inoculation.
Evaluation of apple scab resistance of the Rvi15 cisgenic lines c603, c605, and c606, together with the resistant control GMAL2473 and the susceptible reference ‘Gala’, was performed on grafted greenhouse-grown plantlets following a protocol by Gianfranceschi et al. ( 1996 ). Prior to inoculation, plantlets were grown for 4–6 weeks until they reached the 6–8 leaf stage. Young leaves of at least two actively growing plants per genotype were sprayed with a suspension of V. inaequalis (concentration of approximately 3–5 × 10 5 conidia/mL) and kept at 18 °C and 100% humidity in a tent for 48 h. Then, plants were removed from the inoculation tent to a greenhouse with ~ 70% relative humidity and evaluated 21 days after inoculation. The apple scab resistance tests were repeated four times, with a minimum of three shoots per genotype inoculated in each repetition.
In vitro cultures of the transgenic apple lines carrying Rvi15 (t603, t604, t605, and t606) were provided from Schouten et al. ( 2014 ). None of the four transgenic lines was found to carry pMF1 backbone sequences adjacent to the T-DNA LB (data not shown). The cisgenic lines were regenerated from these transgenic lines via an induction step in which transgenic explants are cultured on a dexamethasone-amended medium that induces R recombinase activity (Vanblaere et al. 2011 ). The recombinase excises the cassette carrying the transgenes, as confirmed by PCR for the absence of the NptII gene (data not shown). Copy-number quantification via qPCR estimated a single integration of the Rvi15 gene in lines c603, c604, c605, and c606 (Fig. 1 ). Fig. 1 Estimation of the number of T-DNA insertion events in the new cisgenic apple lines. Boxplot representation of the qPCR-calculated copy-number ratios of Rvi15 (left) and FB_MR5 (right) in cisgenic lines, compared to genotypes carrying a single copy of the corresponding gene (GMAL2473 for Rvi15 (Galli et al. 2010 ) and C44.4.146 for FB_MR5 (Kost et al. 2015 )). The untransformed cultivar ‘Gala’ (Gala_vitro) served as a negative control. Data were generated using three biological replicates, each tested in technical triplicates
Estimation of the number of T-DNA insertion events in the new cisgenic apple lines. Boxplot representation of the qPCR-calculated copy-number ratios of Rvi15 (left) and FB_MR5 (right) in cisgenic lines, compared to genotypes carrying a single copy of the corresponding gene (GMAL2473 for Rvi15 (Galli et al. 2010 ) and C44.4.146 for FB_MR5 (Kost et al. 2015 )). The untransformed cultivar ‘Gala’ (Gala_vitro) served as a negative control. Data were generated using three biological replicates, each tested in technical triplicates
The insertion sites were successfully identified in each line using TLA. TLA is a targeted sequencing approach that specifically sequences the cisgenic event and its flanking genomic DNA using primers designed on the cisgenic sequence and proximity ligation of DNA fragments near the cisgenic insertion event. Lines c603 and c604 share the same T-DNA insertion site on linkage group (LG) 16, indicating that the originating transgenic lines t603 and t604 were not independent events. Consequently, c604 was excluded from further analyses. Resequencing of the T-DNA genomic junctions at the LB extremity in five independently regenerated cisgenic sublines (c603.1–5) from t603 revealed identical sequences (Fig. 2 ), confirming the reproducibility of recombinase-based cassette excision. Fig. 2 Alignments of sequences from the re-sequenced T-DNA-genomic junctions at the left border extremity of five cisgenic sublines (c603.1–5) derived from t603. The sublines were regenerated independently following excision of the transgenic cassette in the transgenic line t603. Chromatograms are shown with each sequenced sample as well as a consensus sequence (1 st element). The T-DNA-genome junction sequences were aligned to a sequence of the expected structure at the LB, with a red bar indicating T-DNA LB trimming and partial loss of the Rs recombination site. A vertical line indicates the junction between the remaining T-DNA extremity (left) and the adjacent genomic sequence (right)

In lines c605 and c606, the T-DNA was inserted on LG 5 and LG 14, respectively (Table 1 ). For line c606, no sequences adjacent to the T-DNA RB could be retrieved. Amplification and sequencing of the T-DNA-genomic junctions of c603 and c605 revealed near-complete trimming of the RB, leaving up to 73 bp of non-endogenous sequence between the RB and Rvi15 5’-UTR. Similarly, trimming of 34–60 bp was observed at the opposite T-DNA extremities in c603, c605, and c606, leaving up to 92 bp of non-endogenous sequence, mainly consisting of the 81 bp recombinase recognition sequence Rs. T-DNA integration caused deletions of 40 bp and 285 bp of genomic sequences in lines c603 and c605, respectively. In all inoculation experiments with V. inaequalis in the greenhouse, the Rvi15 cisgenic lines, as well as the resistance donor GMAL2473, reacted with a hypersensitive defense response (pinpoint pits), the typical defense reaction of Rvi15 genotypes, while the untransformed genotype ‘Gala Galaxy’ showed sporulation (Fig. 3 ). No sporulation and pinpoint pits were observed on all the three cisgenic lines c603, c605, and c606, confirming the apple scab resistance conferred by Rvi15 . Scale bars are directly indicated in the image. Hypersensitive reactions (pinpoint pits) were observed in all Rvi15 lines and the donor, while only the susceptible control ‘Gala’ displayed sporulation. Leaves were stained for microscopy imaging according to Galli et al. ( 2010 ). Three independent Agrobacterium -mediated transformations were performed using the pMF1:: FB_MR5 vector using 614 ‘Gala Galaxy’ leaf explants. A total of 32 transgenic lines were regenerated, of which 7 showed backbone integration as indicated by positive PCR amplification (data not shown). Three transgenic lines (t47, t49, and t53) were selected for excision of the transgenic cassette, resulting in cisgenic lines c47, c49, and c53. qPCR targeting FB_MR5 indicated a single insertion in the lines c47 and c53, while the cisgenic line c49 carried two insertions (Fig. 1 ).
TLA confirmed the number of insertions and identified the insertion site of FB_MR5 on chromosome 11 for c47 and on chromosomes 8 and 9 for c49. No insertion site could be retrieved for c53. As in Rvi15 lines, T-DNA extremities trimming was observed. Non-endogenous sequences of 38 bp at the RB and up to 163 bp at the LB were detected (Table 1 , Suppl. Fig. S2 ).
In three independent shoot inoculation experiments with E. amylovora , all cisgenic lines c47, c49, and c53 showed significantly reduced symptom severity, measured as percentage lesion length three weeks after inoculation, compared to the highly susceptible wild-type ‘Gala Galaxy’ (Fig. 4 ). Fig. 4 Boxplot representation of the percent lesion length 21 days after inoculation with E. amylovora . Cisgenic lines c47, c49, and c53 carrying FB_MR5 are compared to the control ‘Gala Galaxy’ (GG). n: number of inoculated shoots
Boxplot representation of the percent lesion length 21 days after inoculation with E. amylovora . Cisgenic lines c47, c49, and c53 carrying FB_MR5 are compared to the control ‘Gala Galaxy’ (GG). n: number of inoculated shoots
This study demonstrates the successful application of the cisgenic approach to improve the resistance in the commercial apple cultivar ‘Gala’ against two major diseases in apple orchards, apple scab and fire blight. The disease resistance levels attained were high and comparable to those reported in earlier studies investigating the same resistance genes FB_MR5 and Rvi15 (Kost et al. 2015 ; Schouten et al. 2014 ). Through Agrobacterium -mediated transformation, T-DNA carrying either Rvi15 or FB_MR5 was inserted predominantly as single copies in the majority of cisgenic lines. TLA successfully identified insertion sites in two of three cisgenic lines per resistance gene, confirming random T-DNA integration on different chromosomes, and consistent with qPCR-based copy-number estimates. Sequences on both ends of the T-DNA were trimmed during the insertion process, as previously reported by others (Vanblaere et al. 2014 , Kost et al. 2015 , Dalla Costa 2020). Recombination-driven excision of the transgenic cassette in line t603 was successful, although not only the LB sequence but also approximately one-third of the restriction recombination site was removed. Resequencing of five cisgenic sublines obtained from five independent recombination events from t603 confirmed that recombination worked consistently with no sequence variation among the sublines. The length of vector-derived sequences remaining in the final cisgenic products using the pMF1 vector ranged between 38 and 73 bp at the RB and from 63 to 163 bp on the LB. These numbers are in line with those reported previously for pMF1 (Vanblaere et al. 2014 ) and are lower than the vector-based sequences observed using the p9-Dao-FLPi vector. For example, in line C44.4.146, 94 bp and 359 bp of vector-derived sequences were retained at the RB and LB, respectively (Kost et al. 2015 ). As long as the development of cisgenic lines depends on a recombinase requiring recognition sequences, at least one copy of the recombination site (34 bp for FRT, 81 bp for Rs) will remain in the final product. Dalla Costa et al. ( 2020 ) proposed using an inducible CRISPR/Cas system to avoid recombinase recognition sequences. However, the authors reported that even this strategy would leave a minimum of 37 bp of non-endogenous sequences in the final product (Dalla Costa et al. 2020 ).
Non-endogenous sequences, whether vector-derived or transgenic, may remain in the final product and raise a regulatory concern. If regulators establish a threshold for such sequences based on their length, cisgenic plants could be categorized alongside conventional GM plants or exempted from certain parts of the authorization assessment process. Another potential criterion for exemption could be the precise targeted insertion of the cisgene into a specific genomic locus. However, achieving cisgenic plants free of non-endogenous sequences and ensuring targeted insertion often present a conflict, as non-endogenous sequences, as Lox66 or FRT1 recombination sites, are necessary to facilitate cisgene insertion by e.g., Primeroot editing technology (Sun et al. 2024 ) and are left in the final product.
Our previous research showed that the tissue culture process itself can induce unintended phenotypic deviations. Specifically, the wild-type genotype ‘Gala Galaxy’ used to generate cisgenic line C44.4.146 (and the FB_MR5 lines described here) had altered fruit coloration with reduced red overcolor (Schlathölter et al. 2023 ). This highlights the importance of monitoring somaclonal variation, especially in cultivars whose desirable traits may rely on mutations in specific meristematic layers (Foster & Aranzana 2018 ). It is important to assess if such phenotypic deviations also occur in different in vitro lines of the same cultivar.
To improve the durability of the disease resistance achieved by cisgenesis, and similarly to the approaches used in conventional breeding, several resistance genes targeting the same disease should be deployed in pyramids within the same genotype (Kellerhals et al. 2009 ). FB_MR5 , Rvi15 , Rvi12 , and Rvi6 have limited durability, as shown by the emergence of virulent pathogen strains that overcome these resistances (Emeriewen et al. 2018 ; Parisi et al. 1993 ; Parravicini et al. 2011 ; Patocchi et al. 2020 ; Vogt et al. 2013 ). Additional apple scab resistance genes should be identified in the near future, as their cloning is ongoing (Nadeesha Lewke et al. 2019 ). For fire blight, FB_MR5 remains the only cloned gene to date, but the cloning of FB_E from ‘Evereste’, and FB_Fu from Malus fusca was initiated (Emeriewen et al. 2018 , 2021 ; Parravicini et al. 2011 ). In conclusion, combining strategies to ensure resistance durability through gene pyramiding, minimizing non-endogenous sequences, and ensuring the phenotypic stability of the in vitro plant material will allow the development of cisgenic lines with high fruit quality and durable disease resistance, contributing to the reduction of plant protection product use in apple production and avoiding yield losses.

title: Robust apple leaf disease diagnosis for sustainable horticulture: overcoming background noise with a multilayer transformer-based approach
text:
Apples are one of the most economically significant and widely cultivated fruit crops worldwide, contributing substantially to food security and the horticultural economy. However, their production is frequently compromised by diseases such as Alternaria leaf spot, Apple Mosaic, Powdery Mildew, and Apple Scab, leading to significant yield losses and increased dependence on chemical control. Timely and accurate disease diagnosis is critical to minimize crop damage, reduce pesticide usage, and promote sustainable horticultural practices. This study proposes the Multilayer Transformer-based Apple Disease Classification (MTADC) model, an advanced deep learning framework designed for early and robust identification of apple leaf diseases. MTADC employs a two-stage learning approach: global feature extraction using a transformer encoder, followed by class-specific mapping through a refined classification head. By incorporating a self-attention mechanism, the model effectively suppresses background noise and enhances feature discrimination, even under variable field conditions. Unlike existing models that require well-constrained, high-quality images captured under ideal lighting and angles, MTADC is designed for deployment in real-world field conditions, allowing disease detection from diverse and unconstrained field images commonly captured by farmers. Experiments on a curated dataset comprising publicly available and field-acquired images demonstrate that MTADC achieves a classification accuracy of 96.3%, outperforming conventional convolutional models. These results highlight the model’s robustness, scalability, and potential to be an accessible tool for digital plant health monitoring and precision horticulture.
Apples (Malus spp.) are a cornerstone of global horticulture and one of the most widely cultivated and consumed fruit crops worldwide. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), global apple production has reached approximately 90 million metric tons in recent years, with China, the United States, Poland, and India being major producers 1 , 2 . Apples play a vital role in food security and human nutrition due to their rich content of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants, which contribute to the prevention of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and cancer. Beyond their nutritional significance, apples are economically important in temperate regions, supporting rural livelihoods and contributing billions of dollars annually to global trade 3 , 4 . Although apples can grow in a range of soil types, they prefer well-drained, fertile loamy soils. However, apple productivity is severely threatened by various diseases that reduce yield and fruit quality, thereby affecting marketability and profitability. Alternaria leaf spot, Apple Mosaic, Powdery Mildew, and Apple Scab are among the major diseases affecting apple crops (Fig. 1 ), and these are discussed in detail below:

The United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that to fulfil future food demands, agricultural production must be increased by 70% by 2050. Studies indicate that plant diseases account for approximately 26% of primary yield loss and 38% of secondary yield loss globally, posing a significant challenge to sustainable agricultural practices 5 . In the case of apples, the effective identification and management of the diseases are therefore critical to ensuring high-quality apple production and meeting the growing global demand for this nutrient-dense fruit. Early disease identification and natural treatment are essential components of effective disease management. Appropriate action cannot be taken without accurate identification of apple leaf diseases. Moreover, late identification of these diseases often necessitates increased use of pesticides, posing greater risks to both the environment and human health. Early detection and classification of these diseases are essential to minimize losses, reduce the frequency of chemical sprays, and ensure sustainable production. The traditional approach to managing apple diseases relies majorly on manual inspection and applying chemical pesticides. While these methods have been somewhat effective, they are neither sustainable nor precise. Manual inspection is labour-intensive, time-consuming, and often prone to errors, especially over large orchards. On the other hand, excessive and indiscriminate use of chemical pesticides poses serious environmental and human health risks, including soil degradation, water contamination, and the emergence of pesticide-resistant pathogens.
Recent advancements in machine learning and computer vision have opened new avenues for addressing these challenges. Automated disease detection systems offer a promising alternative by enabling rapid, accurate, and scalable identification of plant diseases. However, implementing machine learning algorithms in agriculture (especially for disease detection and classification) in many countries worldwide has yet to receive considerable attention. Identification of plant diseases is a crucial and practical issue in agriculture because, during the growth phase of a plant, it shows many forms, and it becomes quite challenging to understand the symptoms of a disease. With this aim, researchers are trying to develop different machine learning-based models for detecting and identifying crop diseases in their early stages. However, using advanced deep learning-based models for crop disease (especially for apple crops) identification is still missing in the literature 6 – 9 . This motivated us to develop a novel deep learning-based model that can accurately detect and classify apple crop diseases in their early stages. Moreover, the great success of the vision transformer for image analysis task 10 also motivated us to develop a new Multilayer Transformer based Apple Disease Classifier (MTADC). The proposed MTADC offers unparalleled crop disease detection and classification capabilities by harnessing the power of advanced image analysis techniques. The proposed model allows individuals from diverse backgrounds to leverage its capabilities within the agriculture field. The major limitation of the current methodologies is that they require a properly constrained image of the leaves for accurate classification. Current models are pretty sensitive to background noises and require specific lighting and angles. However, in the field, it is not feasible to capture such high-quality images by the farmers. Essentially, the focus is on designing a model that doesn’t require stringent environmental conditions or specialized expertise to operate effectively. This work aims to detect and classify apple diseases, focusing on four prevalent diseases: Apple Mosaic, Powdery Mildew, and Apple Scab, using the proposed MTADC model.

A domain-specific multilayer Transformer architecture (MTADC) is proposed for apple leaf disease classification under unconstrained field conditions. Unlike standard Vision Transformer and hybrid CNN–Transformer frameworks, the proposed architecture directly models global contextual dependencies using multilayer self-attention, improving robustness to background noise and illumination variability. A lightweight incremental positional encoding-based Patch Encoder module is introduced to enhance computational efficiency for limited agricultural datasets. The proposed encoding strategy reduces patch interaction complexity and enables stable learning without requiring large-scale pretraining, making it suitable for resource-constrained agricultural applications. A multilayer attention learning strategy is developed to extract discriminative disease-specific features while suppressing irrelevant background information. This hierarchical attention mechanism improves feature–disease mapping and enhances classification accuracy in noisy field environments. A real-world apple disease image dataset comprising 1144 field-acquired images collected under uncontrolled orchard conditions at ICAR-Central Institute of Temperate Horticulture, Jammu and Kashmir, India is curated and integrated with public datasets. This dataset enables domain-adaptive training and provides a realistic benchmark for evaluating model robustness in practical horticultural scenarios.

Since the introduction of the deep convolutional network of AlexNet by Krizhevsky et al., 11 , deep learning has made an unprecedented breakthrough in the development of computer vision applications. It has also been widely used in identifying and diagnosing plant diseases due to its better extraction and robustness. Recent literature in disease classification showcases advancements in machine learning techniques such as Transformer, CNN, and Ensemble Learning methods for accurate and automated diagnosis 12 , 13 . A discussion of popular deep learning-based crop disease detection and classification is presented below.
DenseNet-121 model 14 with multi-label classification and improved regression method was proposed by Zhong and Zhao 15 for Apple leaf disease recognition. This model used a focus loss function to identify apple leaf diseases. This achieved 93.51% accuracy on the test set, which was better than the traditional multi-classification method 14 based on cross-entropy loss function with an accuracy of 92.29% using only DenseNet. This research also demonstrated a dynamic way for faster convergence of the model. To speed up model convergence, this article used the pre-training weights of DenseNet 121.
Jiang 16 proposed a model for the recognition of four rice leaf diseases based on CNN and support vector machine (SVM). In this, CNN is used to extract the rice leaf disease features the SVM follows to classify and predict the specific disease. The optimal parameters of SVM are obtained through the 10-fold cross-validation approach. This paper emphasizes that spot color is one of the important criteria for agricultural experts to identify rice diseases 17 . Therefore, in this model image colors have been used as the distinguishing feature. They used a more intuitive way to separate colours provided by Yang et al. 18 . They extracted the colour feature of lesion images in RGB, HSI, and YCbCr colour space to distinguish the colour feature. The experimental results show that this work obtained an accuracy of 96.8% for different rice disease classifications which is higher than that of the traditional back propagation neural networks models. The limitation of this work is that the model required noise-free images which makes it impractical for real world images.
An alternate study by Rao et al. 19 aimed to detect and classify Grape and Mango leaf diseases, employing a dataset of 8438 images of diseased and healthy leaves collected from the Plant Village dataset. This study focused on the utilization of transfer learning of pre-existing models. Kunduracioglu 20 utilized ResNet Architectures for Identification of Tomato Diseases, and Kunduracioglu and Pacal 21 used EfficientNet models for disease detection in Sugarcane leaves. A pre-trained CNN architecture called AlexNet 11 is employed for automatic feature extraction and classification, and the refined deep CNN is trained to identify diseases. This model is trained to first classify the input as healthy or unhealthy leaves and then further classify the type of disease in unhealthy leaves. This model achieved an average accuracy of 94%, with the accuracy range varying across classes from 89% (in Mango’s class) to 99% (in Grape’s class). However, this is clear that this approach is not suitable in the general scenario as without additional tuning, the accuracy will vary vastly across multiple classes.
Further, another work by Rangarajan et al. 22 was proposed using transfer learning with slight customization. Here, the Visual Geometry Group (VGG-16) model 23 was taken as a base model and customized some hyperparameters for fine-tuning the model for their dataset. VGG16 with pre-trained parameters was used for the experiment. The last fully connected layer of the VGG16 had been modified according to the number of disease classes. In this case, the number of neurons in the last fully connected was modified to five which is the number of disease classes. There are several hyperparameters that have been fine-tuned to obtain a trained model that performs better for the disease classification. It produced an accuracy of 94.3% for different brinjal disease classifications. The accuracy of this model fell significantly when images had higher incident angles of sunlight.
After this, the improved ResNet Based Apple Leaf Diseases Identification model was proposed 24 . This work used the ResNet18 25 classification network as a baseline. As the symptomatic area of some leaf diseases can be small, a Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM) 26 was considered to improve the feature representation ability. The CBAM is a lightweight attention module that can be embedded into CNN, and introduces approximately negligible amount of computation and parameters. It can improve the recognition ability of the apple leaf disease classification model. Their ResNet-CBAM model achieved an accuracy of 95.2% on a dataset crafted within a controlled scientific environment. However, in a real-world scenario, farmers cannot produce images of such quality, limiting the above model’s performance.
Another generalized model proposed by Paymode and Malode 27 , utilized the VGG model 23 to detect the grapes and tomato leaves disease in the early stage. This method also utilized the concept of multi-class labeling, where it first classified the leaves as healthy or diseased. Then within the diseased class, it identified the particular disease. The pre-trained weights of the VGG model are used to train the model which achieved a varying range of accuracy from 95.71% for tomatoes and 98.4% for grapes. This method indeed offers a versatile model applicable across multiple crops. Nevertheless, its accuracy is significantly hampered by the pervasive issue of noisy datasets. This compels a reliance on manual intervention or other suitable techniques to effectively eliminate noise before inputting the image into the model. This step becomes pivotal in ensuring the model’s accuracy and reliability in real-world applications.
A distinct report by Zhang et al. 8 , 9 used a pre-trained Siamese dilated Inception network (SDINet) 28 as a base network. The dilated Inception module is introduced into AlexNet 11 to construct two subnetworks for SDINet, and two subnetworks are responsible for extracting multi-scale features from image pairs in the same layer. The global pooling instead of the fully connected layers is utilized to reduce the number of model parameters without any feature loss. SDINet is trained with image pairs, each consisting of two real diseased leaf images or one real disease and one healthy leaf image. The SDINet makes full use of the advantages of multi-scale dilated Inception to enrich and improve the information and enhance the adaptability of the model. Unlike the existing deep CNNs, SDINet used cosine distance learning to calculate the similarity between the leaf image pairs to recognize apple diseases. This model can work efficiently with few training samples and is suitable for smaller datasets. This model achieved an accuracy of 94.17% without needing a large dataset. However, the performance of this model in real-world scenarios is not devoid of degradation due to environmental factors. This model is incapable of extracting the features from those images which are captured under an uncontrolled environment.
Recent advances in computer vision have demonstrated the effectiveness of Transformer-based architectures for image classification tasks, including plant disease detection. Vision Transformer (ViT) models utilize self-attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies and global contextual information, which is particularly advantageous for complex visual scenes in agricultural environments 10 . Several studies have reported that Transformer-based models exhibit improved robustness to illumination variations, background clutter, and occlusions in agricultural image analysis.
Hybrid CNN–Transformer architectures have also been developed to combine the strong local feature extraction capability of convolutional neural networks with the global contextual modeling ability of Transformers. Architectures such as Swin Transformer 29 , ConvNeXt 30 , and DeiT 31 have achieved competitive performance in plant disease recognition tasks, while EfficientNet-Transformer variants have demonstrated improved computational efficiency.
Compared with these general-purpose architectures, the proposed Multilayer Transformer-based Apple Disease Classification (MTADC) model is specifically tailored for field-level apple disease detection under unconstrained imaging conditions. Unlike conventional ViT frameworks that require large-scale pretraining and computationally intensive positional encoding strategies, MTADC incorporates a lightweight incremental positional encoding mechanism and multilayer attention learning designed for limited agricultural datasets. Furthermore, while hybrid CNN–Transformer models exploit convolutional inductive biases for local feature extraction, MTADC focuses on hierarchical self-attention to capture global contextual dependencies relevant to complex orchard environments. The model is trained on a hybrid dataset comprising field-acquired and public images, enhancing robustness to background noise and illumination variability.
Deployment of deep learning models in real-world agricultural environments often leads to performance degradation due to uncontrolled imaging conditions, including background clutter, illumination variability, occlusions, and sensor noise. Training models under unconstrained field conditions is therefore essential for practical disease diagnosis. Zhang et al. 8 , 9 proposed a multi-scale deep learning framework for apple leaf spot detection in unconstrained environments, achieving an accuracy of 85.23%, demonstrating the feasibility of field-deployable disease detection systems. Recent studies have also explored various apple disease detection approaches, including the Simple Linear Iterative Clustering combined with the Kennard–Stone algorithm for apple mosaic disease detection 6 , 7 , Siamese dilated Inception networks for apple disease recognition 8 , 9 , and multi-scale constrained deformable convolutional networks for apple leaf disease classification 6 , 7 . These models have shown promising performance under controlled experimental settings; however, their robustness under real-world field conditions remains limited.
Consequently, there is a growing need for domain-specific Transformer-based frameworks capable of handling complex background noise and illumination variability encountered in practical horticultural settings. The proposed MTADC model is designed to address these challenges through multilayer self-attention mechanisms and domain-adaptive training on mixed field and public datasets.
The proposed MTADC framework is inspired by the Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture; however, it is not a direct implementation of ViT. MTADC incorporates domain-specific architectural adaptations, including incremental positional encoding, hierarchical feature aggregation across transformer layers, and a deployment-oriented optimization pipeline. These modifications are designed to improve robustness for real-field agricultural images characterized by background noise, illumination variability, and class imbalance. Therefore, MTADC should be viewed as a domain-adapted transformer framework rather than a generic ViT model. The detailed step by step working of the proposed MTADC model is shown in Fig. 2 . As can be seen from Fig. 2 , the proposed model begins by taking an image as an input, which is then divided into multiple patches. These patches are flattened into one-dimensional vectors, converting each 2D patch into a single row of pixel values. Next, each vector undergoes a linear transformation, which maps it to a higher dimensional space. This increases the number of elements in each vector, allowing the model to capture more detailed and complex information from the patches, making them ready for further processing. After that, positional encoding is applied to each patch.
This encoding embeds spatial information into the patches, which helps the model to understand their relative positions within the image. Next, the patches and their positional encodings are passed into the Transformer Block. Within the transformer block, attention scores are calculated and applied 32 . These attention scores allow the model to focus on relevant patches and capture global dependencies. This process is repeated for each layer of the transformer block, as specified. Finally, after multiple iterations through the transformer block, the features learned by the MTADC model are aggregated and refined. These features are then mapped to their respective classes using dense layers. The dense layers act as a classifier, interpreting the learned features and assigning probabilities to each class, ultimately determining the most likely class for an input image. The primary goal of the proposed model is to classify an image, not to convert the image into any other form, which can be implemented through the encoder part only. Hence, the multilayer transformer of the proposed model does not have a decoder part.
The proposed MTADC model is a multilayer transformer model in which attention scores are calculated at multiple levels. It has multiple sub-modules that work together to accomplish the task (Fig. 3 ). To ensure clarity regarding the interconnection between modules, state notation (i.e., S1, S2, ..., S5) is utilized to depict that the output of each module, denoted by a specific state, is exclusively forwarded to the subsequent module in the system. The Patch Encoder module (Fig. 4 ) is designed to generate image patches and incorporate positional information into each patch representation. The input image is first partitioned into non-overlapping patches to enable the transformer model to learn spatial relationships and inter-patch dependencies. In this study, the input image of size 256 × 256 is divided into 256 patches of size 16 × 16. This patch size provides an appropriate balance between spatial resolution and computational efficiency. Since transformer architectures are permutation invariant, positional information must be injected into the patch embeddings to preserve spatial structure. Therefore, positional encoding is added to each patch embedding to provide spatial context 33 . Based on learning from the Transformer Block, dense layers are designed to extract information indicating which class the disease predominantly resembles. The Transformer Block focuses on identifying the features present in the image, while the dense layers synthesize this information to determine the most appropriate class assignment. In essence, the Transformer Blocks perform feature extraction, while the dense layers consolidate these features to make a classification decision. The initial and intermediate fully connected dense layers have a variable number of neurons, while the last output layer has neurons equal to the number of output classes. The neurons in these layers provide the details of what the MTADC model has learned, i.e., the features of a particular class of the disease. These are the weights that are learned by the proposed MTADC model during training. The output (O) is obtained from the model by combining all the information across various dense layers (Eq. ( 11 )).
For apple disease classification experiments, a hybrid dataset consisting of field-acquired and publicly available images was curated. Field images were collected from the experimental apple orchard of ICAR–Central Institute of Temperate Horticulture (ICAR-CITH), Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India (Latitude: 33.98° N; Longitude: 74.80° E), under unconstrained field conditions, including natural illumination variations, occlusions, and background clutter. These field-acquired images correspond to three disease categories: Alternaria, Apple Mosaic Virus, and Powdery Mildew. To increase dataset diversity and include an additional disease class, publicly available Apple Scab images were obtained from a Kaggle repository, consisting of 4748 images. After quality filtering and preprocessing, the final dataset comprised 4748 images across four disease classes: 274 Alternaria, 208 Mosaic, 180 Powdery Mildew, and 4086 Scab images (Fig. 1 ). The dataset is inherently imbalanced, reflecting realistic field conditions where disease incidence varies across classes. Specifically, field-acquired images constituted 662 samples (Alternaria, Mosaic, and Powdery Mildew), while publicly sourced images accounted for 4086 samples (Apple Scab). This strategic combination of field and public datasets enhances variability in imaging conditions and enables evaluation of the model’s robustness under both controlled and real-world scenarios. Class imbalance was retained intentionally to evaluate the ability of the proposed MTADC model to generalize under skewed class distributions commonly encountered in practical horticultural monitoring applications.
To ensure uniformity and improve model convergence, all images were resized to a fixed resolution of 256 × 256 pixels. This resolution provides a balance between computational efficiency and preservation of disease-related visual features. Pixel intensities were normalized to the range [0, 1] by dividing by 255 to stabilize gradient-based optimization and accelerate training convergence. To prevent data leakage, the dataset was first split into training and testing subsets using an 80:20 stratified ratio. The training subset was further divided into training and validation sets in a 70:30 ratio. Data augmentation was applied only to the training set to increase sample diversity and mitigate overfitting. Augmentation operations included random rotations within ± 60° and shearing transformations with a magnitude range of 0 to 0.2. Through augmentation, the effective training dataset size was increased fourfold, resulting in 18,992 training samples. Given the inherent class imbalance in the dataset, no oversampling was applied to preserve the real-world disease distribution. Instead, the robustness of the proposed MTADC model under skewed class distributions was evaluated using multiple performance metrics, including accuracy, precision and F1-score. This approach reflects realistic orchard disease prevalence and evaluates model generalization in practical horticultural scenarios.

The first thing for implementation of the model is the data preprocessing. We started with applying an appropriate process to preprocess the dataset and apply augmentations to introduce variety in our dataset. The model underwent multiple training sessions with different sets of hyperparameters to explore various configurations and optimize the performance of the model. This process in volved experimenting with combinations of hyperparameters to determine the most effective settings for achieving high ac curacy. Ultimately, after thorough testing, it was determined that a specific set of hyperparameters resulted in optimal performance, yielding a training accuracy of 97% and a testing accuracy of 96.32%. The model is tested on a different number of heads (as shown in Table 1 ) and various Optimizers (as shown in Table 2 ). Finally, the best set of hyperparameters i.e., Number of heads = 2, and Optimizer = Adam, are selected for the proposed MTADC model.

To assess the model’s saturation point and its ability to learn from the data, an extended training session was conducted for 50 epochs (as shown in Figs. 6 and 7 ) using the final set of hyperparameters. Early training fluctuations (epochs 10–20) arise from optimization instability, noisy gradients, and the model’s initial adaptation to complex data patterns. Curves stabilize post-epoch 30 as learning converges, with validation accuracy plateauing. Training/validation losses align near zero after epoch 25, showing no overfitting and good generalization via dropout and controlled complexity—yielding minimal gains beyond 30 epochs. Beyond this point, there were no substantial improvements observed in the accuracy metrics, indicating that the model had effectively learned the underlying patterns and features in the data (Fig. 8 ). This analysis of saturation helps in understanding the optimal training duration for the proposed MTADC model, ensuring efficient use of computational resources and avoiding un necessary training iterations that do not significantly enhance performance. The above graph provides a comprehensive view of the proposed MTADC model’s performance throughout the training process. This includes accuracy and loss plotted against the number of epochs during the training of the model. The results obtained from this training phase are then evaluated using an independent testing dataset. This testing set contains instances from various classes present in our dataset, and it is used to assess how well the proposed MTADC model generalizes to new, unseen data. When testing the proposed MTADC model on this unknown dataset, we analyze its performance across different classes (as shown in Table 3 ). This analysis involves examining metrics accuracy across each class individually. These metrics provide insights into how effectively the model can classify instances belonging to different classes, and what are the possible classes of images the proposed MTADC model is confusing into.

To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed MTADC framework, comparative experiments were conducted using representative convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures widely employed in plant disease classification studies. Specifically, VGG16 and ResNet were selected as pre-trained baseline models due to their established performance and widespread adoption in agricultural image analysis. Additionally, a custom CNN architecture was implemented to provide a lightweight baseline and to analyze the impact of handcrafted convolutional feature extraction.
Transfer learning was employed for VGG16 and ResNet by initializing the models with ImageNet pre-trained weights, followed by fine-tuning on the apple disease dataset. The custom CNN model was trained from scratch with randomly initialized weights. All baseline models were trained and evaluated on the same dataset splits to ensure a fair and consistent comparison with the proposed MTADC model.
Although recent architectures such as EfficientNet and Vision Transformer variants have demonstrated promising performance in large-scale vision tasks, they typically require extensive training data and computational resources, which are often limited in agricultural research settings. Therefore, the selected baselines provide a realistic and reproducible benchmark for evaluating the performance gains introduced by the proposed Transformer-based MTADC framework.

Accuracy is a fundamental metric used to evaluate the performance of machine learning models. It represents the proportion of correctly predicted instances among all instances in a dataset. A high accuracy score indicates that the model is making accurate predictions overall. Performance evaluation and comparison of the different models with their optimized hyper parameters and accuracy achieved is shown in Table 4 . Class-wise accuracy, on the other hand, provides a more de tailed view of the model’s performance by evaluating accuracy on aper-class basis. This metric is particularly useful in scenarios where the dataset is imbalanced, meaning some classes have significantly fewer instances than others. In such cases, overall accuracy can be misleading, as a model might perform well on the majority class but poorly on minority classes. Class-wise accuracy helps identify these disparities and provides insights into how well the model is performing for each individual class. Since the dataset utilized for this model has some significant variation in a number of images per class, so class wise accuracy helps to further analyze and compare our results. We can see that the proposed MTADC model outperforms various other models (as shown in Fig. 9 ), in a majority of the classes, some differences being quite significant, whereas some are quite close because some features are better captured by CNN local feature extraction but as a whole, our MTADC outperforms other models and architecture by a significant amount (Table 5 ).

The F1score is a metric commonly used in machine learning to evaluate a model’s performance, especially in binary classification tasks. It combines precision and recall into a single value, providing a balanced measure that considers both false positives and false negatives. A high F1 score indicates that the model has a good balance between precision (the proportion of true positive predictions among all positive predictions) and recall (the proportion of true positive predictions among all actual positive instances). The F1 score is particularly useful when dealing with imbalanced datasets, where one class dominates the data, as it takes into account the model’s ability to correctly identify both positive and negative instances. By using the F1-score, all model’s overall performances are evaluated to devise an informed conclusion that the proposed MTADC model is comparatively more efficient in real-world scenarios for apple leaf disease classification than other models (Table 6 ). The MTADC model consistently outperforms or matches competing models across all disease classes in terms of F1-score. Its performance is particularly notable for Powdery Mildew and Scab, where it demonstrates a clear edge over CNN, ResNet, and VGG-16. CNN shows competitive results for Mosaic and Scab but struggles for Alternaria and Powdery Mildew. ResNet and VGG-16 consistently exhibit lower F1 scores, making them less reliable for apple disease classification tasks.
Precision is a crucial metric in machine learning that measures the accuracy of positive predictions made by a model. It quantifies the proportion of true positive predictions among all instances predicted as positive by the model. A high precision score indicates that the model makes fewer false positive predictions, which is important in scenarios where the cost of false positives is high, such as in our case where false prediction can lead to incorrect treatment. Precision is particularly valuable when dealing with imbalanced datasets or when the focus is on the performance of positive predictions. It complements other metrics by providing insights into the model’s ability to avoid false positives and make accurate positive predictions. By evaluating precision, all model’s reliability for positive predictions is evaluated and the conclusion is devised that the proposed MTADC model is most suitable for the cause as compared to other models (Table 7 ). The MTADC model demonstrates outstanding precision for Powdery Mildew and Scab, while maintaining competitive performance for Alternaria and Mosaic. CNN occasionally surpasses MTADC in Alternaria and Mosaic precision, but its performance drops considerably for Powdery Mildew. ResNetandVGG-16generallylagbehind across all disease categories, suggesting their limited suitability for this task.
Accuracy curves display the progression of model accuracy over training epochs, showcasing how well the model is learning to make correct predictions. On the other hand, loss curves illustrate how the loss function changes during training, indicating how effectively the model minimizes the errors. Comparing these curves across different models it was found that the VGG16 and ResNet model initially performed well but over time there is quite a downfall and they saturated to lower accuracy, however in case of CNN it saturated early within 10 epochs whereas our multilayered transformer model took 30 epochs to saturate however the proposed MTADC model produced the most optimal result among all models tested. During the training of VGG16 and ResNet models, it was found that the models were training well for a few epochs and then there was a large downfall in accuracy and an increase in the loss. Around 10 epochs the models appeared to be converged however slight further training showed that the model was not converging and after prolonged training, we found that these models converged around 40 epochs. However, the CNN model and the proposed MTADC do not show such a pattern, and they converge without such downfalls. There are multiple noises in the background, and thus, while training, there is a possibility that the model may learn some noise features, resulting in reduced accuracy of the model. The multilayer transformer model is countering this by using multi head attention, and thus, there are no such downfalls in the proposed MTADC model. Moreover, the CNN model does not have multiple complex layers as in VGG16 and ResNet, so in CNN also, no such downfalls are observed.
The robustness of the proposed MTADC framework was evaluated using a hybrid dataset containing both field-acquired and public images captured under diverse environmental conditions. Field images were collected under natural orchard settings, exhibiting variations in illumination, background clutter, occlusions by branches and fruits, and partial leaf damage. Furthermore, data augmentation operations such as rotation and shearing were applied to simulate additional geometric distortions and occlusions. The proposed model demonstrated stable performance across all disease classes, indicating strong robustness against real-world imaging variability. These results suggest that MTADC can generalize effectively under practical horticultural monitoring scenarios.
Overall, the proposed MTADC model outperforms other models (as shown in Fig. 9 ) across all the classes. The results clearly establish the proposed MTADC model as the most robust and effective solution for apple leaf disease classification. Its high precision and F1-scores across all four disease classes, particularly for Powdery Mildew and Scab, highlight its superior ability to accurately classify diseases while minimizing false positives and negatives. CNN shows some strengths, particularly in Mosaic and Scab, but its performance drops noticeably for other diseases. ResNet and VGG-16 lag significantly behind, making them less suitable for this task. The MTADC model’s consistent performance and balanced results across precision and F1-score make it the most reliable choice for real-world disease detection in apple crops. The difference in performance is quite significant across all of the classes. Performance of other models were acceptable in some of the specific classes, but poor in other, which is not the case with the proposed MTADC model.
Fig. 10 Flow of information in real time.
Flow of information in real time.
Although the proposed MTADC framework demonstrates strong performance, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the model was trained on four apple disease categories, and its ability to generalize to unseen disease classes remains to be explored. Second, the field-acquired dataset was collected from a specific geographic region, and variations in apple cultivars, orchard management practices, and environmental conditions across different regions may affect model performance.
Furthermore, extreme illumination conditions, severe occlusions, and sensor-specific artifacts were not systematically evaluated in this study. Future research will focus on large-scale multi-region data collection, domain adaptation, and continual learning strategies to improve generalization across diverse agro-climatic zones and apple varieties. Incorporating open-set recognition and few-shot learning frameworks could further enable detection of previously unseen disease patterns, enhancing the practical applicability of the proposed system.
The model is designed for real-world practical application i.e. to assist the farmers specifically smartphones with constrained compute resources and unreliable internet access. With the advancement and wide avail ability of the mobile phones, they are accessible to each and every hand. They serve as the ideal platform to deliver this solution to those in the agricultural sector. To facilitate this, a mobile application has been developed that act as an intermediate for accessing the model. The app features multiple interfaces (as depicted in Fig. 10 ) that allows users to upload images. Once an image is uploaded, it is transmitted to a server where the proposed model is hosted for processing.
Fig. 11 Interface of the application.
Interface of the application.
The server processes the image by passing it through the model, which generates a prediction. This prediction is then sent back to the mobile application, which displays it to the user along with additional relevant details, providing a clear and in formative response. The complete flow of this process, as it happens in real-time, is depicted in Fig. 10 . In this architecture, smartphones serve solely as image capture interfaces (Fig. 11 ), bypassing the need for onboard compute on farmer devices. Captured images transmit to a lightweight central server for inference, delivering reliable performance across diverse rural smartphone hardware. To ensure that the application is user-friendly and hassle-free, the prediction process needs to be as fast as possible. Delays in response time can reduce the effectiveness of the app, especially in real-world scenarios with high number of users. However, ensuring this kind of speed and efficiency for a large number of users, presents significant challenges. This is because scaling the application to support many users would require deploying multiple high-performance servers capable of handling the computational load of a resource-intensive machine-learning model. For small organizations, this is not a feasible option, as acquiring and maintaining such infrastructure demands substantial investment.
In general, the weights are stored in float32 format. By using quantization, we are converting the weights from higher memory format to lower memory formats. However, using lower formats (like int8) reduces the accuracy of the model. Thus, the proposed model is tested upon various quantizations, along with other standard model for comparison. 100 pictures are directly taken from the apple orchards using 64MP mobile camera. The proposed model is uploaded on a low-end server with 2GB RAM and only integrated GPU. The other model is also uploaded on same server for comparison purpose.
To assess practical deployment viability, we evaluated inference latency and computational demands in the same low-resource environment and reported in Table 8 . Latency was averaged over 100 field-captured orchard images from a 64 MP smartphone camera. The float32 baseline MTADC model took ~ 185 ms per image, dropping to ~ 132 ms (16-bit) and ~ 94 ms (8-bit) post-training quantization, enabling near real-time agricultural decision-making.

Precision format Model accuracy Avg. inference latency (ms/image) Memory footprint (MB) Deployment suitability Float32 (baseline) 96.32% 185 ms 118 MB Cloud/server deployment Float16 quantized 94.00% 132 ms 61 MB Edge server/moderate devices Int8 quantized 91.00% 94 ms 32 MB Edge devices/mobile feasible
Comparison of inference latency and computational demands in the same low-resource environment.
The float32 model demanded ~ 118 MB memory during inference, while 16-bit and 8-bit versions cut this to ~ 61 MB (48% reduction) and ~ 32 MB (73% reduction), respectively. These gains ease server loads and support deployment on affordable hardware for smallholder farmers.
In the current setup, smartphones handle image capture, with inference on a lightweight central server. This hybrid approach offloads computation from farmer devices, ensuring robust predictions amid diverse hardware and rural connectivity. Quantized MTADC also holds promise for future on-device inference via TensorFlow Lite or ONNX Runtime Mobile.
Observed inference latency enables predictions within one second under moderate network conditions, ensuring usability in connectivity-limited rural settings. Further, from the Table 8 , it is inferred that, the proposed MTADC model is suitable for the deployment at edge devices. As compared to other models the loss in accuracy of the proposed model is not too significant even at 8bit quantization. This is due to the distribution of information across various layers of the model. These characteristics make the proposed system suitable for scalable deployment through farmer-accessible smartphones without requiring specialized hardware.
In this work, a Multilayer Transformer-based Apple Disease Classification (MTADC) model is presented for robust and accurate classification of different apple leaf diseases in their early stages. The proposed MTADC model has demonstrated exceptional performance and surpassed established models like CNN, ResNet, and VGG16. Through rigorous training and hyperparameter tuning, we achieved an impressive accuracy of 96.32% on the testing set, with class-wise accuracies ranging from 92.84% to 99.58%. The stability of MTADC model’s training process, converging around 30 epochs, reflects its efficient learning capabilities. Our transformer architecture, with its Patch Encoder, transformer blocks, and dense layers, not only delivers superior accuracy but also offers scalability for potential enhancements. This model’s success opens doors for practical applications, particularly in fields like agricultural disease detection (evidenced by high accuracy across classes like Alternaria, Mosaic, Mildew, and Scab), where accurate image classification is paramount. The Multi Layer architecture of the presented model has not been explored to its maximum limit. The proposed model is presented only for the apple plants. However, to advance its reach in agriculture field, the model is required to be trained and tested across various variety of crops. As a future work, to fully utilize the proposed model’s capabilities, it needs to be analyzed on a wider domain of crops. The deployment-oriented design of MTADC enables practical adoption in real-field conditions through smartphone-assisted disease diagnosis.
