title:
Enhanced Disease
Resistance Mechanism of the CmoAP2/ERF
Transcription Factor in Pumpkin through Genetic Mutations
text:
The squash species Cucurbita moschata has been historically utilized by both animals and humans as a food
source. It is an annual dicotyledonous vegetable known for its health
benefits, including reducing the risk of various diseases, such as
cancer, high blood pressure, diabetes, intestinal disorders, and atherosclerosis,
in humans. However, the cultivation of this valuable crop is often
challenged by diseases such as powdery mildew (PM), caused by the
fungus Podosphaera xanthii . PM not
only reduces yield but also impacts photosynthesis rates. A newly
identified gene called CmoCh3G009850 , which encodes
the transcription factor known as AP2-like ethylene-responsive factor
(CmoAP2/ERF), has been marked for resistance against PM. A shift in
the state from susceptible to resistant can be induced by nonsynonymous
SNP mutations at five locations of the CmoCh3G009850 gene. The dynamical studies of the wild-type (WT) and mutated-type
AP2/ERF proteins’ interactions with DNA were explored by docking
and molecular dynamics simulation studies. These five mutations T105A,
S302R, H321R, H335D, and V402A are incorporated in the AP2/ERF transcription
factor that makes a stable and compact complex with DNA rather than
the WT protein. Overall, the identification and characterization of
the CmoAP2/ERF gene and its variants represent a
significant advancement for the breeding and cultivation of C. moschata varieties resistant against powdery mildew.
This study not only enhances our understanding of plant–pathogen
interactions but also provides a potential avenue for developing more
resilient squash varieties through genetic improvement.
Pumpkin ( Cucurbita moschata ) is
a versatile and widely cultivated edible plant enjoyed both as a vegetable
and for its medicinal properties across various regions, including
Europe, Asia, and parts of the Americas. The plant is valued not only
for its fruits but also for its seeds and greens, making it an important
multifunctional food source. 1 In terms
of nutrition, pumpkin is noted for its low-fat content, high protein
richness, and good antioxidant compounds, which makes it a favorable
choice for dietary inclusion, especially in regions where protein
sources may be limited. 2 , 3
Beyond its nutritional value,
pumpkin has gained significant attention
in the medical field due to its bioactive compounds. These compounds
exhibit a wide range of health-promoting properties, including anti-inflammatory,
antiparasitic, antimicrobial, anticarcinogenic, antioxidant, antidiabetic,
hepatoprotective, and hypotensive. 4 , 5 These diverse
health benefits underline the potential of pumpkin as a functional
food and a natural source of bioactive compounds with therapeutic
properties. Its widespread cultivation and consumption in various
cultures highlight its nutritional and medicinal significance globally.
Plants have developed regulatory mechanisms to adapt against the
dynamic changes in the environment that affect their survival, growth,
and reproduction. Globally massive agricultural losses have resulted
due to various abiotic stresses. 6 These
environmental factors, such as high salinity, water scarcity, and
extreme temperature, affect particular plant hormone signaling pathways
and are controlled through specific hormones and transcription factors
belonging to these stress responses. Under abiotic stress, plants
produce several hormones such as ethylene (ET) and abscisic acids
(ABAs), which are produced as stress hormones, while gibberellins
(GAs), brassinosteroids (BRs), and cytokinins (CTK) are produced in
different amounts to promote plants’ growth. Changing these
substances facilitates the best responses to be achieved. 7 During abiotic stress, these hormones are regulated
by hormone- and stress-responsive transcription factors. 8 The transcription factor belonging to the APETALA2/ETHYLENE
RESPONSIVE FACTOR (AP2/ERF) family is now recognized as an important
modulator of numerous abiotic stresses along with multiple hormone
responses for managing external stress in plants 9 and regulating fruit development. 10 Some biomarkers are linked with control of biotic 11 , 12 and abiotic stress in the plants and are responsible for several
diseases in human beings, like breast cancer. 13
The first reported ERF domain as a conserved motif in four
DNA-binding
proteins in Nicotiana tabacum (tobacco)
is the ethylene-responsive element-binding proteins 1, 2, 3, and 4
(EREBP1, 2, 3, and 4). And now they are renamed as ERF1, 2, 3, and
4, and they interact with the GCC box of DNA sequence. 14 The ERF family in plants is classified into
four subgroups due to ancient transposition, homing process, and tandem
as well as chromosomal/segmental duplication. 15 ERF family proteins have several diverse functions to regulate the
cellular processes in order to control abiotic stresses such as low
temperature, water deficit and drought, 16 − 18 and high-salt- and cold-responsive
conditions. 19 The AP2 or ethylene responsive
element binding factor (EREB) domain of AP2/ERF has 40–70 conserved
amino acids for binding with DNA segments. 15 , 20
The fungus Podosphaera xanthii lowers
the rate of photosynthesis and causes powdery mildew (PM) on pumpkin
leaves. The novel gene belonging to AP2-like ethylene-responsive transcription
factor (CmoAP2/ERF), which is responsible for resistance against PM,
was reported in the genome-wide association study (GWAS) study of
healthy pumpkin seedlings. 21 Nonsynonymous
single nucleotide mutations affect the structural and functional properties
of proteins. 22 Certain protein mutations
termed as disease-causing mutations have been shown to improve susceptibility
or vulnerability, but sometimes these mutations behave oppositely.
The study by Alavilli et al., 2022, focused on the AP2/ERF protein
extracted from a genome-wide association study (GWAS) of pumpkin ( C. moschata ), specifically investigating its role
in resistance against powdery mildew caused by Pseudomonas
xanthii . 100 According to
their findings, five nonsynonymous mutations were identified within
the AP2/ERF protein sequence which were associated with resistance
against this fungal disease. These mutations were hypothesized to
alter the protein’s structure and function, thereby enhancing
its ability to confer resistance. To delve deeper into the molecular
mechanisms behind this resistance, we analyzed the DNA–protein
interaction patterns of both the wild-type (WT) and mutant-type AP2/ERF
proteins. We employed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to observe
the dynamic behavior of these protein–DNA complexes over time.
MD simulations are computational techniques used to model the movements
and interactions of atoms and molecules over a time scale. 23 By subjecting the protein–DNA complexes
to MD simulations, we aimed to elucidate how these mutations affect
the stability and dynamics of the complexes. Specifically, we observed
how the mutated AP2/ERF proteins bind to DNA sequences involved in
regulating the resistance pathways against PM.
The mutations
identified in the AP2/ERF protein are proposed to
play a critical role in regulating these resistance pathways in pumpkins.
By understanding the structural and dynamic changes induced by these
mutations through computational modeling, we provided insights into
how these genetic variations can influence disease resistance in crops
like C. moschata . This knowledge would
be invaluable in future breeding efforts aimed at developing more
resilient pumpkin varieties through targeted genetic manipulation.
The protein sequence
of AP2/ERF was extracted from the Supporting Information of the GWAS study on Pumpkin ( C. moschata ) as published by Alavilli et al., 2022. Since the protein’s
three-dimensional structure was not yet available in the protein data
bank, we used an I-TASSER server to model the protein. 24 , 25 The SAVES server ( https://saves.mbi.ucla.edu/ ) was used for the quality assessment of the modeled structure by
using ERRAT, 26 VERIFY 3D, 27 , 28 and PROCHECK. 29 We performed molecular
dynamics simulation at 50 ns to refine the modeled structure AP2/ERF
using GROMACS 30 ·
DNA sequences
have been obtained from the PDB (PDB id 7WQ5 ), which is bound with an ethylene-responsive
transcription factor WRI1 of Arabidopsis thaliana . 31 Using the HDOCK server, DNA was docked
with the AP2/ERF protein by choosing advanced parameters that specified
the binding site residues, which are based on a template-based docking
procedure. 32 The site-directed mutagenesis
at five residues was carried out by PyMol, and subsequently, the structure
was equilibrated and minimized by GROMACS. 33 − 36 Finally, the mutated minimal
structure was docked with DNA by HDOCK again.
Molecular
dynamics (MD) simulations are a powerful tool for understanding the
dynamic behavior, stability, and flexibility. 37 We performed MD simulations for the wild-type (WT) and mutated AP2/ERF
protein–DNA complexes at atomic resolution, complementing the
experimental techniques. The amber99bsc1 force field was used to simulate
both the WT and mutant protein–DNA complexes. The force field
file was downloaded from the Gromacs Web site. 38 The complexes were solvated in a cubic box with edges of
12.39 Å using the TIP3P water model. The system was neutralized
by adding Na + and Cl – ions, and steric
clashes were resolved through 50,000 iterations of energy minimization
using the steepest descent method with a cutoff of 1000 kJ/mol. Two-phase
equilibration was performed to ensure the stability of the solvent
molecules and ions. The temperature was stabilized using the NVT ensemble at 300 K, and the pressure was equilibrated
using the NPT ensemble at 1 atm, running for 100
ps each. Finally, MD simulations of the WT and mutated protein–DNA
complexes were conducted for 100 ns.
Different dynamics
parameters of complexes were analyzed by modules available in Gromacs
to understand the biomolecular behavior of complexes. It provided
a detailed explanation of the behavior of the atoms in the complexes
over time. First, we indexed the protein–DNA complexes through
the make_ndx module. Four stability parameters, i.e.,
root-mean-square deviation (RMSD), root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF),
the radius of gyration (Rg), and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), 39 were used for the complex analysis. The RMSD,
RMSF, Rg, and SASA were determined by rms , rmsf , gyrate , and sasa modules, respectively. The obtained xvg files were analyzed and
visualized by Xmgrace. 40 Hydrogen bond
distribution is another parameter to determine the stability of the
complex. Therefore, the hbond module was used for
the distribution of hydrogen bonds between the protein and DNA over
time. The structural dynamics of the protein–DNA complex during
MD simulations were investigated by principal component analysis (PCA).
It unravels the collective motions within the protein–DNA complex.
Two modules, covar and anaeig , were
finally used for the PCA.
The protein
sequence of AP2/ERF was obtained from a GWAS study of C. moschata . 21 They observed
that mutation in the AP2/ERF gene was involved in
resistance against the powdery mildew caused by the fungus P. xanthii . The proposed protein
sequence is very unique and does not show homology with any other
proteins present in the PDB database. That is why a three-dimensional
structure was modeled for this protein by threading or ab initio (hybrid)
modeling methods. I-TASSER was used for hybrid modeling of the AP2/ERF
protein sequence ( Figure 1 a). It gave different predicted models using the folds of
various PDB structures ( 7WQ5 , 2OCW , 2NBI , 5FMW , 8WXB , and 5WX9 ).
(a) Modeled three-dimensional
structures of AP2/ERF by I-TASSER.
(b) After simulation; (c) aligned structures before and after simulation;
Ramachandran plot of AP2/ERF structures (d) before and (e) after simulation.
Initially, the modeled protein structure did not meet the criteria
for a good-quality structure. Only 65.2% of residues were within the
allowed regions of the Ramachandran plot, while 27.8% were within
additional allowed regions ( Figure 1 d and Table 1 ). This indicates that a significant portion of the protein
structure deviated from ideal structural conformations. Following
MD simulation, which involved analyzing the RMSD, RMSF, and Rg, it
was observed that the structure became stable over time ( Figure S1 ), and the dimensional confirmation
in the cartoon model is shown in Figure 1 b. The RMSD, a measure of structural deviation
from the starting structure, indicated that the protein structure
stabilized during the simulation. After 50 ns of MD simulation, there
was an improvement in the quality of the modeled structure. Now, 82.5%
of the residues were in favored regions (indicating they were within
favorable conformational parameters), and 14.9% were in additional
allowed regions ( Figure 1 e and Table 1 ). This
suggests that the structure became more closely aligned with the expected
structural norms. Comparing the initial modeled structure with the
structure after MD simulation, the RMSD value was 12.136 ( Figure 1 c). This value indicates
the average distance between equivalent atoms in the two superimposed
structures, reflecting the degree of structural variation between
the initial and the simulated structures.
Proteins’ associated structural topologies support a thorough
analysis of the structural perturbations caused by mutations which
exhibit the pathogen interactions. 41 , 42 The WT AP2/ERF
protein was mutated at five positions, i.e., T105A, S302R, H321R,
H335D, and V402A. For stability and structural minimization, the mutated
structure was simulated at 5 ns. The RMSD value gives information
on the differences between the backbones of the proteins. After mutations,
the RMSD between WT and mutated AP2/ERF protein structures was 3.633
nm. The ratio of residues in the Ramachandran plot region can be seen
in Figure 2 a and the
fourth column of Table 1 . When compared to the WT protein, the mutated structure’s
quality is slightly improved. Three-dimensional conformational changes
in the WT (blue) and mutated (magenta) AP2/ERF proteins are shown
in Figure 2 b. Sequences
of proteins have specific structures and functions defined as motifs,
also termed as supersecondary structures. The reported protein was
491 amino acids long, and they have two major motifs belonging to
the AP2/ERF family ( Figure 2 c).
Pictorial representation of the (a) Ramachandran plot of mutated
AP2/ERF protein, (b) superimposed structures of wild and mutated proteins
(blue–wild type and magenta–mutated type), (c) conserved
motifs, and (d) 3D structure of DNA helix.
The two
most important biological molecules of the cell are proteins and DNA.
The protein–DNA interactions regulate many biological processes
such as cell regulation, DNA replication, signal transduction, protein
synthesis, and many more. Therefore, the docking of protein and DNA
helps us to understand the atomic-level behavior of complexes in the
biological process used to develop a new variety and resistance crop.
The WRINKLED1 (WRI1) regulator is involved in oil synthesis in A. thaliana , and it belongs to the APETALA2 (AP2)/EREBP
transcription family. 31 , 43 The structure of the 24 nucleotide
long DNA sequence (5′-TACTTCCTCGGTTTCATCGTCCAC) was obtained
from the bound form with transcriptional factor WRINKLED1 (PDB: 7WQ5 ).
Figure 3 displays both two-
and three-dimensional depictions of the WT protein–DNA interaction.
Thirteen hydrophobic interactions and seven hydrogen bonds were detected
in the complex. Seven residues (Ser25, Glu27, Arg37, Met74, Gln75,
Arg397, and Thr418) of protein are involved in the formation of hydrogen
bonds with four nucleotides of the 5′ to 3′ strand (5T,
16A, 17T, and 18C) and two nucleotides of the 3′ to 5′
strand (4G and 23T).
WT target protein–DNA docked complex (a) backbone
and base
nucleotide representation, (b) base interaction nucleotide representation,
and (c) 2D representation of interactions (green dotted line for hydrogen
bonds and semicircle for hydrophobic bonds). (a,b) are made by PDIviz
1.24a, 44 and (c) are drawn by LigPlot. 45
The mutant protein–DNA complex’s
interactions (two-
and three-dimensional representations) are illustrated in Figure 4 . The interactions
between the mutated protein and DNA comprise 13 hydrophobic interactions
and six hydrogen bonds. Protein residues Pro338, Gly340, Ser341, His346,
Arg365, and Asn385 build hydrogen bonds with two nucleotides of the
3′ to 5′ strand (6C and 10G) and four nucleotides of
the 5′ to 3′ strand (13T, 14T, 15C, and 21C). Table S1 provides further details, including
additional interaction and surface properties of WT and mutant protein–DNA
complexes.
Mutated target protein–DNA docked complex (a) backbone and
base nucleotide representation, (b) base interaction nucleotide representation,
and (c) 2D representation of interactions (green dotted line for hydrogen
bonds and semicircle for hydrophobic bonds).
The trajectory analysis of the MD simulations for the protein–DNA
complex, before and after mutation, reveals significant insights into
the structural dynamics and stability of the complexes.
Figure 5 a illustrates the
RMSD values of the protein–DNA complexes over a 100 ns simulation
period. The black line represents the RMSD of the wild-type transcription
factor-DNA complex, while the red line corresponds to the mutated
TF-DNA complex. The average RMSD for the wild-type complex (black)
is approximately 1.2 nm, with fluctuations ranging between 0.8 and
1.5 nm. The mutated complex (red) shows a lower average RMSD of around
0.9 nm, with fluctuations ranging between 0.5 and 1.2 nm. Initially,
both complexes exhibit similar RMSD values, indicating comparable
structural conformations. However, as the simulation progresses, the
wild-type complex shows higher RMSD fluctuations, suggesting greater
structural instability. In contrast, the mutated complex maintains
lower RMSD values, indicating enhanced stability. This suggests that
the mutation confers structural rigidity to the protein–DNA
complex, potentially contributing to the observed resistance against P. xanthii .
Trajectory analysis of molecular dynamics simulation
of the protein–DNA
complex before (black) and after (red) mutation, (a) RMSD, (b) Rg,
(c) RMSF of protein, (d) RMSF of DNA, (e) hydrogen bond distribution,
and (f) SASA.
The observed reduction in RMSD for the mutated
complex is consistent
with previous studies indicating that specific mutations can lead
to enhanced structural stability of protein–DNA complexes. 46 , 47 Enhanced stability often correlates with improved functional performance,
particularly in transcription factors where stable binding to DNA
is critical for effective gene regulation. 48
Rg reflects
the compactness of the protein structure. Figure 5 b shows that the Rg for the wild-type complex
fluctuates around an average of 3.0 nm, whereas the mutated complex
maintains a lower average Rg of approximately 2.8 nm. Both complexes
display fluctuations throughout the simulation, but the mutated complex
(red) exhibits a consistently lower Rg compared to the wild-type complex
(black). This decreased Rg for the mutated complex suggests a more
compact and stable structure, further supporting the enhanced stability
observed in the RMSD analysis. A more compact structure may enhance
the ability of the protein to interact with DNA, thereby improving
its functional efficiency in binding to DNA and regulating gene expression
related to powdery mildew resistance.
Compactness, as indicated
by lower Rg values, is often associated with improved protein–DNA
binding affinity and specificity. 49 This
structural compactness can facilitate the proper positioning of critical
residues in the DNA-binding domain, enhancing the transcription factor’s
ability to recognize and bind to its target DNA sequences. 50
The
RMSF analysis, shown in Figure 5 c,d, provides residue-level insights into the flexibility
of the protein and DNA, respectively. For the protein ( Figure 5 c), the wild-type complex exhibits
higher fluctuations across several residues, indicating greater flexibility
and potential instability. The mutated complex, however, shows reduced
fluctuations, particularly in regions critical for DNA binding. For
DNA ( Figure 5 d), the
wild-type complex also demonstrates higher RMSF values, suggesting
a less stable interaction with the protein. The mutation results in
lower RMSF values, highlighting a more stable protein–DNA interaction.
Reduced RMSF values in the mutated complex suggest that the mutation
leads to a decrease in conformational flexibility, thereby stabilizing
the interaction between the protein and DNA. This stabilization is
crucial for maintaining the integrity of the protein–DNA complex
during the dynamic processes of gene regulation. 51 , 52 Enhanced stability in critical binding regions can improve the transcription
factor’s ability to modulate gene expression effectively, contributing
to increased resistance against pathogens such as P.
xanthii . 53
Figure 5 e presents the hydrogen
bond distribution over the simulation period. The wild-type complex
(black) shows an average of 7 hydrogen bonds, with fluctuations indicating
instability. The mutated complex (red) exhibits a higher average of
10 hydrogen bonds with fewer fluctuations, suggesting more stable
interactions. This indicates that the mutation enhances the formation
of hydrogen bonds, thereby stabilizing the protein–DNA interaction
and potentially contributing to the resistance mechanism against P. xanthii .
Hydrogen bonds play a critical
role in stabilizing protein–DNA interactions, and an increase
in hydrogen bonding can significantly enhance the binding affinity
and stability of the complex. 54 , 55 The observed increase
in hydrogen bonds in the mutated complex suggests that the mutation
enhances the intermolecular interactions, thereby stabilizing the
complex and potentially improving its functional performance in gene
regulation. 56
The SASA values, illustrated in Figure 5 f, reflect exposure of the protein–DNA
complex to the solvent. Lower SASA values indicate a more compact
and less solvent-exposed complex. Figure 5 f shows that the SASA for the wild-type complex
(black) is higher, with an average of 410 nm, 2 indicating greater exposure to the solvent. The mutated complex
(red) has a lower average SASA of approximately 390 nm, 2 suggesting reduced solvent exposure and a more
compact structure. This compactness may protect the complex from deleterious
environmental interactions, enhancing its functional stability.
A lower SASA value indicates a more buried and compact structure,
which can enhance the stability of the protein–DNA complex
by reducing the exposure of hydrophobic regions to the solvent. 57 This compactness is likely to contribute to
the overall structural stability and functional efficiency of the
transcription factor in regulating gene expression. 58
The allelic variation in the CmoCh3G009850 gene,
encoding the AP2-like ethylene-responsive transcription factor (CmoAP2/ERF),
appears to play a crucial role in conferring resistance to powdery
mildew in pumpkins. The MD simulation results indicate that the mutation
stabilizes the protein–DNA complex, as evidenced by lower RMSD,
RMSF, and SASA values along with a higher number of stable hydrogen
bonds. This structural stability likely enhances the binding efficiency
of the transcription factor to its target DNA, thereby improving the
regulation of genes involved in defense responses against P. xanthii .
PCA is a powerful statistical tool used to simplify
the complexity of high-dimensional data while retaining most of the
variation in the data set. In the context of molecular dynamics simulations,
PCA helps us to understand the major conformational changes in protein–DNA
complexes. Figure 6 presents the PCA results for the wild-type (susceptible) and mutated
transcription factor (TF)-DNA complexes, providing insights into their
structural dynamics.
Principal component analysis (PCA) of the protein–DNA
complex
before (black) and after (red) mutation. (a) 2D projection trajectory,
(b) projection on eigenvectors, and (c) RMS fluctuation. Eigenvector
components (d) before mutation and (e) after mutation.
Figure 6 a shows
the 2D projection of the trajectory onto the first two principal components
(eigenvectors) for the wild-type (black) and mutated (red) protein–DNA
complexes. The wild-type complex has a broader distribution with projections
ranging from −25 to 25 nm, indicating higher conformational
flexibility. The mutated complex has a narrower distribution, ranging
from −15 to 15 nm, suggesting reduced flexibility and more
restricted motion. This compactness of the mutated complex could contribute
to its increased resistance to P. xanthii by maintaining a stable interaction with the DNA. Reduced conformational
flexibility, as observed in the mutated complex, is often associated
with enhanced structural stability and functional efficiency during
protein–DNA interactions. 59 This
stabilization can facilitate more effective binding and regulation
of target DNA sequences, contributing to the transcription factor’s
role in disease resistance. 60
Figure 6 b presents
the projection of the trajectories on the first two eigenvectors over
the 100 ns simulation period. The wild-type complex shows larger fluctuations
along both eigenvectors, with average projections around ±10
nm for the first eigenvector and ±5 nm for the second eigenvector.
In contrast, the mutated complex exhibits smaller fluctuations, with
average projections around ±5 nm for the first eigenvector and
±3 nm for the second eigenvector. The pronounced fluctuations
in the wild-type complex indicate significant conformational changes,
reflecting its unstable nature. The reduced fluctuations in the eigenvector
projections for the mutated complex indicate that the mutation promotes
a more stable conformational landscape, enhancing the functional performance
of the protein–DNA complex. 61 Stability
in the conformational landscape is critical for the efficient binding
and regulation of DNA by transcription factors. 62 This further supports the notion that the mutation leads
to structural rigidity and stability, which could be crucial to its
functional role in resistance mechanisms.
Figure 6 c illustrates
the RMSF values for the protein–DNA complexes, highlighting
the flexibility of each residue. The wild-type complex has higher
RMSF values, particularly in critical regions for DNA binding, with
average RMSF values around 0.6 nm and peaks reaching 1.0 nm. The mutated
complex shows reduced RMSF values, with averages around 0.4 nm and
peaks reaching 0.8 nm, indicating increased rigidity and stability
in these regions. This stabilization likely contributes to the efficient
binding of the transcription factor to its target DNA, facilitating
the effective regulation of genes involved in powdery mildew resistance. Figure 6 d,e displays the
contributions of individual atomic components to the first and second
eigenvectors before and after mutation, respectively. The black line
represents the total motion, while the red, green, and blue lines
correspond to the x , y , and z components of the motion, respectively. The wild-type
complex shows higher variability in the contributions, with fluctuations
ranging from −0.1 to 0.1 for the first eigenvector and from
−0.05 to 0.05 for the second eigenvector. The mutated complex
exhibits more consistent and lower variability in the eigenvector
components with fluctuations ranging from −0.05 to 0.05 for
the first eigenvector and −0.03 to 0.03 for the second eigenvector.
This reduction in motion is indicative of a more rigid and stable
protein–DNA complex, which is likely to enhance its functional
efficiency in resisting P. xanthii .
The PCA results provide compelling evidence that the allelic variation
in the CmoCh3G009850 gene encoding the AP2-like ethylene-responsive
transcription factor (CmoAP2/ERF) plays a pivotal role in stabilizing
the protein–DNA complex. The mutation leads to a more compact,
stable, and less flexible complex, as demonstrated by the reduced
RMSF values, lower projections on eigenvectors, and focused 2D projection
trajectory. 63 These structural characteristics
are likely to enhance the binding affinity and specificity of the
transcription factor to its target DNA, thereby improving the regulation
of genes involved in defense responses against powdery mildew in pumpkin.
Several species of fungi, bacteria, viruses, and oomycete affect
crop yields through the process of host–pathogen interactions.
There is a list of fungi which cause various diseases like Alternaria cucumerina (Alternaria leaf blight), 64 Cercospora citrullina (Cercospora leaf spot), 65 Pseudoperonosporacubensis (downy mildew), 66 Fusarium
solani (Fusarium crown and foot rot), 67 Fusarium oxysporum , 68 Didymella bryoniae (gummy stem blight), 69 Erysiphe spp. (powdery mildew), 70 Septoria cucurbitacearum (Septoria leaf spot), 71 Sclerotium rolfsii (southern blight), 72 and Verticillium dahliae (Verticillium wilt). 73 Bacteria such
as Pseudomonas syringae (angular leaf
spot), 74 Erwinia tracheiphila (bacterial wilt), 75 as well as some viruses,
for example, cucumber mosaic virus (cucumber mosaic) 76 and watermelon mosaic virus (watermelon mosaic), 77 cause serious
diseases which directly affect crop yields. Phytophthora
capsici (Phytophthora blight) and Phytophthora
melonis ( Phytophthora blight) are
oomycetes that act as pathogens responsible for the crown and fruit
rotting in pumpkin ( Cucurbita pepo ),
significantly affecting the yields of crops. 78 − 81
It is anticipated that
using pathogen-resistant cultivars will
boost the yield while reducing the need for fungicides in farming.
The essential components of the plant defense system that combat various
pathogens are transcription factors. 82 The
AP2/ERF family, a crucial transcription factor that has two tandem
AP2 domains that bind to a dsDNA region, has emerged as the most viable
option for bioengineering to increase the yield by improving the resistivity.
The 3-D structure and function of proteins are determined by the
amino acid patterns. 83 The folding, stability,
interaction of the protein with other molecules, and overall functionality
of the protein can all be affected by alterations in the amino acid
sequences. 84 − 87 The structure and functions of the proteins can be changed when
the amino acids have been mutated at specific sites, like conserved
residues; otherwise, the mutation can change its structure but does
not affect protein function. These mutations in the amino acids are
a result of DNA markers like SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphism)
and changes at single positions in plants’ DNA. 88 Finding different SNPs that can be used to build
new products is now easier because of recent technological advancements.
It demonstrates how SNPs in the gene’s functional regions can
alter the expressed region to regulate the levels of biotic and abiotic
stress while improving the crops’ variety resistance to both. 89
Compared to the WT protein, the pumpkin
mutant AP2/ERF protein
binds more strongly with the DNA, leading to a more stable complex.
The molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the WT transcription
factor-DNA complex is less stable and shows significant instability
during the simulation process. This instability likely contributes
to the pumpkin’s susceptibility to fungal infection. Conversely,
the enhanced stability of the mutant protein–DNA complex suggests
its role in activating various pathways that improve resistance to
fungal infection. These findings are consistent with studies such
as of Murmu and Archak (2024), 90 where
the mutant form of a protein was reported to form a more stable complex
than its WT counterpart, which exhibited instability. Similarly, Panchal
et al. (2020) 91 observed that mutations
in the XPD gene led to altered protein stability, highlighting the
importance of structural changes in influencing functional outcomes.
Pumpkins are extremely
valuable crops that are predominantly utilized
globally as food items and rootstocks for cucurbits. Still, P. xanthii hampers pumpkin growth and reduces the
level of plant production. A molecular explanation is provided by
the in silico investigation of the transcription factor AP2/ERF’s
interaction with DNA. The enhanced resistance capabilities against
the fungal infection can be credited to the mutated structure, which
is more stable than the WT protein, and the same has been confirmed
in the present study by docking and MD simulation studies of WT and
mutant protein complexes. The combined trajectory analysis and PCA
reveal that the mutation in the CmoAP2/ERF gene significantly
impacts the structural dynamics of the protein–DNA complex.
The mutation results in a reduced conformational flexibility, increased
stability, and more coordinated motions within the complex. These
changes will likely enhance the functional efficiency of the transcription
factor in regulating genes involved in powdery mildew resistance.
The findings from these analyses highlight the potential of targeted
genetic modifications in the development of resistant crop varieties.
Future studies should include experimental validation through in vivo
experiments to confirm these computational predictions and further
elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying powdery mildew resistance
in pumpkins.

in this study are available in this article and the accompanying Supporting Information .

title: Identification of Powdery Mildew Resistance-Related Genes in Butternut Squash (Cucurbita moschata)
text:
Powdery mildew infection is a significant challenge in butternut squash ( Cucurbita moschata ) production during winter in Hainan, China. The tropical climate of Hainan promotes powdery mildew infection, resulting in substantial yield losses. By utilizing transcriptome and genome sequencing data, SNPs and potential genes associated with powdery mildew resistance in butternut squash were identified. The analysis of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) following powdery mildew infection revealed several genes involved in resistance, with particular focus on a resistance (R) gene cluster that may be linked to the observed resistance. Two MLO genes in clade V from Cucurbita moschata may not be directly associated with resistance in the two genotypes studied. These findings are expected to contribute to the development of genetic tools for improving powdery mildew resistance in Cucurbita crops, thereby reducing yield losses and enhancing the sustainability of butternut squash production in Hainan and other regions.
Butternut squash is a genotype of Cucurbita moschata , known for its robust branching habit and hammer-shaped fruits with a sweet, nutty flavor, making them suitable for roasting and steaming. The mini-type butternut squash has gained increasing popularity in the Chinese market because of its convenience, portability, and extended shelf life. Hainan Province, located in the southernmost part of China and surrounded by the South China Sea, has a tropical climate and is the main vegetable production area, including butternut squash, for the mainland Chinese market, particularly during winter. Although Hainan experiences milder winters than other regions of China, the combination of relatively low temperatures, high humidity, and limited sunlight during this period creates favorable conditions for the outbreak of powdery mildew, which significantly affects butternut squash production. Incomplete statistics suggest that powdery mildew can lead to yield reductions of 30–70% in Hainan, causing economic losses amounting to hundreds of millions of yuan annually (Yun, personal communication). Therefore, understanding the genetics of powdery mildew resistance and developing resistant cultivars may be the most effective strategy to alleviate this issue in Hainan.
The primary powdery mildew species infecting Cucurbita species is Podosphaera xanthii . As a biotrophic pathogen, powdery mildew fungi rely on living cells and tissues of the host plant for nutrition. After invading the epidermal cells of the host, it forms haustoria, which allows it to absorb nutrients from the host plant cells [ 1 ]. Previous studies have identified multiple powdery mildew resistance genes, among which the R gene-mediated resistance response triggers localized programmed cell death in the host plant, limiting the spread of powdery mildew as a biotrophic pathogen, thereby achieving immune effects [ 2 ]. The Mla locus, conferring resistance to powdery mildew in barley, is believed to be tandemly arranged with three typical R genes that have an NBS-LRR structure [ 3 , 4 , 5 ]. The SGT1 gene is an essential component mediating R gene-mediated plant disease resistance signaling pathways [ 6 ]. Therefore, mutations or silencing of the SGT1 gene can lead to the loss of R gene-mediated disease resistance, resulting in susceptibility. Its overexpression can enhance HR response and improve powdery mildew resistance [ 7 ]. The RPW8 gene found in Arabidopsis may enhance salicylic acid-dependent basal defense against powdery mildew by inducing programmed cell death [ 8 ]. Among all homologous chromosomes in wheat, as many as 100 QTLs related to powdery mildew resistance have been detected [ 9 , 10 ]. Because of the incomplete expression of some major R genes, the combined participation of minor resistance genes, and other multigenes, as well as the influence of the environment, powdery mildew disease resistance ultimately manifests as a quantitative trait [ 11 ].
In addition, previous studies on powdery mildew resistance have identified a susceptibility gene that participates in plant immune responses [ 12 ]. One of the most well-known is the MLO gene (Mildew resistance locus o) [ 13 ]. The loss-of-function mutant ( mlo ) forms localized cell wall deposits, preventing the powdery mildew spores from penetrating the host’s epidermal cells to form haustoria and hyphae, thereby blocking further infection by powdery mildew fungi [ 14 , 15 ]. In barley, mlo -based powdery mildew resistance mutants have been successfully used commercially on a large scale, with over half of the spring barley varieties in Europe containing the mlo gene, exhibiting complete resistance to powdery mildew, and this resistance has remained durable over the decades [ 16 ]. As more genomes were sequenced, it became clear that MLO genes are part of a large gene family, all encoding seven transmembrane proteins, and have diversified into several clades with different functions in plants [ 17 , 18 ]. The mlo genes involved in powdery mildew resistance in monocots like barley and wheat are in clade IV, while in dicots, they belong to clade V [ 17 ]. The MLO gene was also found to play an important role in response to PM in cucumbers and other cucurbit crops. In cucumber, a MLO ( Csa5G623470 ) in clade V, linked to the locus pm5.1 , has been identified as the causal gene for durable powdery mildew resistance [ 19 ]. The same loss-of-function mutation MLO genes ( Csa5G623470 , named CsaMLO8 ) was proven to cause hypocotyl resistance to PM [ 20 ]. The other two MLO genes in clade V were also cloned, and overexpression of all three CsaMLO genes in the tomato mlo mutant restored susceptibility to PM to a different extent [ 21 ].
Several genetic studies have identified loci associated with resistance to powdery mildew in Cucurbita [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ]. Among these, the Pm-0 locus, which was considered introgressed from a wild Cucurbita species, provides resistance to powdery mildew in commercially cultivated Cucurbita varieties [ 23 , 24 ]. This locus contains several candidate genes that might together contribute to resistance [ 23 ]. Another major dominant locus CpPM10.1 in zucchini contains an Arabidopsis RPW8 domain after fine mapping [ 27 ]. The MLO genes in clade V of Cucurbita species were identified and shown to exhibit differential expression between resistant and susceptible plants [ 28 , 29 ]. In this research, we aim to identify the possible powdery mildew resistance-related genes from transcriptome data after powdery mildew infection and to analyze the overall diversity and SNPs of the two genotypes of squash using genome sequencing data. Reliable SNPs identified within and between the two butternut squash genotypes can be utilized for genetic mapping. Analyzing differentially expressed genes after powdery mildew inoculation in the two squash genotypes will enhance our understanding of the genes involved in powdery mildew resistance and provide genetic tools for improving resistance in Cucurbita .
The genotype ‘YD26’ exhibited significantly lower incidence and severity of powdery mildew infection compared to ‘SF02’ ( Figure 1 A). The leaves of YD26 showed minimal symptoms, with only sporadic occurrence of white powdery spots observed on leaves and stems. In contrast, SF02 plants displayed widespread infection, with prominent white powdery lesions covering substantial portions of leaf surfaces
Throughout the experiment, YD26 plants maintained vigorous growth with minimal impact from powdery mildew. Conversely, SF02 plants exhibited stunted growth, leaf chlorosis, and reduced vigor because of severe powdery mildew infestation. Statistical analysis of disease scoring between YD26 and SF02 on day 10 (240 hpi) confirmed the significant differences in powdery mildew resistance ( Figure 1 B). The average infection score for 14 YD26 plants was 1.86, while for 16 SF02 plants, it was 3.75. A significant difference in the disease index was observed between YD26 and SF02, with YD26 exhibiting notably higher resistance, as confirmed by a t -test analysis ( p = 0.00077).
SNPs and InDels variations derived from whole genome and transcriptome sequencing data are provided in Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 . Comparative analysis of SNP mutations between YD26 and SF02 revealed distinct genomic profiles, as illustrated in Supplementary Figure S1A . YD26 displayed 94,910 heterozygous SNP sites alongside 481,678 homozygous SNP sites, resulting in a heterozygosity ratio of 16.46%. In contrast, SF02 had a higher heterozygosity ratio of 33.23%, with 187,969 heterozygous SNP sites and 377,686 homozygous SNP sites. YD26 showed a total of 576,588 SNPs, including 372,776 transitions and 192,879 transversions, while SF02 had 565,655 SNPs, comprising 379,341 transitions and 197,247 transversions. Both genotypes displayed similar trends in SNP mutation types, with T:A > C:G and C:G > T:A mutations being the most common, while C:G > G:C mutations were least frequent.
A comparative analysis of SNP variation across genome-wide and coding sequence (CDS) regions between YD26 and SF02 revealed both similarities and notable differences (see Supplementary Figure S1B ). YD26 showed slightly fewer SNPs in intergenic regions (138,506) compared with SF02 (153,324) and in upstream gene regions within 5 kilobases (124,114) compared with SF02 (124,314). Conversely, YD26 had a slightly higher count of SNPs in downstream gene regions within 5 kilobases (92,413) compared with SF02 (90,169). Additionally, YD26 exhibited a higher count of synonymous coding mutations (28,843) compared with SF02 (28,228). In addition to the overall differences between the two genotypes, we conducted the following detailed analysis of genetic variations within specific potential candidate genes that might contribute to the observed differences.
Analysis of the transcriptome sequencing data revealed distinct gene expression patterns in both YD26 and SF02 genotypes before inoculation with powdery mildew (0 h post-inoculation, 0 hpi). A total of 716 genes showed significant differential expression, with adjusted p -values below 0.05 and an absolute log2FC > 0.5, as detailed in Supplementary Table S3 . Of these 716 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), 344 were upregulated and 372 were downregulated, as illustrated in Figure 2 A. Under non-inoculated conditions, several genes in YD26 exhibited upregulated expression compared with SF02, suggesting their potential roles in underlying molecular pathways. Notably, CmoCh18G013170, annotated as a G-type lectin S-receptor-like serine/threonine-protein kinase and homologous to Arabidopsis At5g24080, emerged as the most prominently upregulated gene. Additionally, within the top ten DEGs, CmoCh06G007400, identified as a putative disease resistance protein RGA4, and CmoCh16G004710, annotated as a pathogen-related protein-like, indicated potential involvement in disease resistance mechanisms.
Moreover, the gene CmoCh02G016340, annotated as a two-component response regulator-like APRR2 and associated with fruit color regulation in several gourd species, also exhibited differential expression. YD26 showed downregulation of this gene compared with SF02. In contrast, SF02 had higher expression of top-ranking DEGs such as CmoCh18G008700 (F-box protein, SKIP5 ) and a probable leucine-rich repeat receptor-like protein kinase, homologous to Arabidopsis At1g35710. Gene Ontology (GO) annotation of all DEGs revealed the top 10 categories in Biological Process (BP), Cellular Component (CC), and Molecular Function (MF), as shown in Figure 2 B. Top annotations include processes such as oxidation–reduction, transmembrane transport, and secondary metabolite biosynthesis. These findings show genotype-specific differences with certain genes expressed exclusively in either YD26 or SF02, indicating potential genetic variations related to the response to powdery mildew.
Thousand more DEGs compared with 716 DEGs at non-infection (00 hpi) were induced in response to powdery mildew infection in both YD26 and SF02 genotypes at 6 and 24 h post-inoculation (hpi), as shown in Figure 3 A,B. At 6 hpi, YD26 exhibited a unique gene expression profile with 56.2% of its DEGs differing from the non-infection baseline (00 hpi), which is notably higher than the 30.4% observed in SF02. The total number of DEGs, both shared between the two genotypes and specifically expressed in each, increased at 24 hpi compared with 6 hpi, reflecting the greater number of genes induced as the infection progresses.
The gene expression fold change profiles are visualized in the scatter plots ( Figure 3 C,D). In YD26, approximately 2967 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified, with around 1585 DEGs upregulated and 1372 DEGs downregulated at 6 hpi. In contrast, SF02 had 566 upregulated and 448 downregulated specific DEGs, totaling 1014. Among the 2311 shared DEGs, most exhibited similar up- or downregulation patterns between the two genotypes. However, 14 genes (highlighted in purple) displayed opposite expression patterns, including genes such as peroxidase, proteinase inhibitor, phytohormone-binding protein, ABC transporter B family member, and two-component response regulators. Additionally, 65 genes exhibited expression differences of at least twofold, as indicated by their position outside the dotted lines in the plots. Notable among these are leucine-rich repeat receptor-like protein kinase, cytochrome P450, and pathogenesis-related proteins, which are strongly associated with disease resistance.
At 24 h post-inoculation (24 hpi), both YD26 and SF02 exhibited an increased number of genes involved in defense against powdery mildew. The number of shared DEGs with opposite expression patterns rose to 45. These include genes such as MYB6-like transcription factor (CmoCh20G009160), phytohormone-binding protein-like (CmoCh16G008570), JUNGBRUNNEN 1 transcription factor (CmoCh12G002210), ethylene-responsive transcription factor ABR1-like (CmoCh04G025710), and a probable calcium-binding protein (CmoCh09G02150). Additionally, the number of genes showing at least a twofold expression difference increased to 307. These include receptor-like protein kinase FERONIA (Cmo14Ch011870), WRKY transcription factor 22-like (CmoCh16G006300), MLO-like protein 2 (Cmo18Ch008900), probable calcium-binding protein CML10 (CmoCh12G004850), ethylene-responsive transcription factor ERF011-like (CmoCh01G018820), and several leucine-rich repeat receptor-like protein kinases (CmoCh16G001430, CmoCh02G017590, CmoCh15G014460), as well as cytochrome P450s (CmoCh10G000910, CmoCh18G006850). These genes are strongly implicated in the defense response to powdery mildew.
DEGs that exhibit significant differences starting at 00 hpi and maintain either upregulation or downregulation across subsequent time points may be correlated with powdery mildew resistance ( Figure 3 E,F). Notably, nine specific genes—CmoCh06G007420, CmoCh06G007410, CmoCh06G007400, CmoCh06G007390, CmoCh06G007380, CmoCh15G012680, CmoCh18G001720, CmoCh18G001710, and CmoCh19G000350—demonstrated consistent expression patterns, as shown in Supplementary Figure S3 . Among these, a cluster of five adjacent genes on chromosome 6, spanning CmoCh06: 3,817,738 to 3,836,887 ( Figure 4 A), includes one cytochrome P450 gene and four disease resistance gene analogs (RGAs). These genes consistently exhibit expression in YD26. In contrast, SF02 shows no detectable expression for four out of these five genes. To further validate these findings, RT-qPCR was performed to assess the expression of these genes. Data analysis, normalized using the 2 ΔΔCT method, revealed significant differences in expression levels. Specifically, the four adjacent genes showed notable expression in YD26, whereas no expression data were available for SF02 ( Figure 4 B).
A total of 20 MLO family gene sequences were identified from C. moschata resequencing and transcriptome data. Based on the distribution of MLO genes in C. moschata chromosomes, these 20 MLO family genes were named CmoMLO1 to CmoMLO20. Among the 20 CmoMLO genes, they are distributed on 15 out of the 20 chromosomes of C. moschata . Chromosomes 2, 3, 4, 13, and 20 each contain two Mlo genes. The sizes of the CmoMLO genes in squash vary, with the number of exons ranging from 13 to 15. The CDS of these genes, which encode proteins of approximately 500 amino acids in length, are detailed in Supplementary Table S4 .
Phylogenetic analysis was performed on MLO protein sequences from butternut squash, along with sequences from Arabidopsis thaliana , cucumber, and functional MLO genes from the following four monocotyledonous crops: barley ( HvMLO ), wheat ( TaMLO ), rice ( OsMLO ), and maize ( ZmMLO ). The protein sequences used for this analysis are listed in Supplementary Table S5 . The phylogenetic tree was constructed using the maximum likelihood method following multiple sequence alignment with MEGA7.0. The MLO gene sequences were classified into seven clades and labeled I to VII. MLO genes from Arabidopsis , cucumber, and butternut squash were grouped into all six branches except clade IV. All functional MLO proteins associated with resistance to powdery mildew in barley, wheat, rice, and maize were grouped into clade IV ( Supplementary Figure S4 ).
In the transcriptome data of two different squash materials with different resistance levels sampled at different time points after powdery mildew inoculation, the expression levels of 20 MLO family genes were analyzed based on the FPKM values ( Figure 5 A). Among these genes, CmoMLO7 consistently exhibited significantly higher expression compared with the other MLO genes in both resistant and susceptible materials. CmoMLO7 showed a notable increase in expression at 6 h (h) and 24 h (h) post-inoculation, followed by a gradual decline after 48 h (h). In contrast, the expression levels of other MLO genes remained relatively low and showed no significant changes before or after inoculation. Since CmoMLO7 and CmoMLO18 are closely related and both belong to clade V, we examined their expression using real-time qPCR in the two squash genotypes. The relative expression patterns for both genes showed no significant differences between the genotypes at various time points ( Figure 5 B) and reflected the same trends as the FPKM values from the transcriptome data.
Powdery mildew significantly impacts the fruit quality and productivity of C. moschata and other commercial Cucurbita species [ 30 , 31 ]. The inherent genetic resistance of Cucurbita species to powdery mildew is occasionally detected in C. moschata and is usually absent in C. pepo [ 23 , 27 , 32 ]. Nevertheless, in both species, resistance has been effectively achieved by introgression of a key resistance locus, named Pm-0 , obtained from a resistant wild Cucurbita species, C. okeechobeensis subsp. Martinezii , which is used widely in breeding and found in nearly all commercial powdery mildew resistance C. moschata and C. pepo . The locus Pm-0 is considered responsible for resistance in nearly all powdery mildew resistance commercial cultivars of squash, pumpkin, and zucchini. Linkage mapping identified that the Pm-0 locus within a 76.4 kb interval contained 14 candidate genes on LG10 [ 23 ]. Since the publication of the C. moschata genome [ 33 ], we found the locus Pm-0 located on chromosome 3, CmoCh03: 7,539,988~7,620,164, based on the sequences of two flanking markers. Seventeen genes are located on the interval. According to our transcriptome data, only one gene, CmoCH03G010130, appeared in the list of 716 differentially expressed genes under non-inoculated conditions ( Supplementary Table S1 ). CmoCH03G010130 is annotated as Cyclin-H1-1 with cyclin-dependent protein serine/threonine kinase regulator activity. This gene might have broad gene function rather than a direct connection with powdery mildew, as no publication has associated it with powdery mildew.
Other candidate genes in this interval that are highly likely to be involved in powdery mildew disease resistance include CmoCh03G010060, which is the homolog to At5G66900, an NBS-LRR protein in Arabidopsis thaliana that contains a domain similar to the RPW8 locus known for conferring resistance to powdery mildew, and CmoCh03G010010, annotated as peroxidase 10. Additionally, CmoCh03G010100, annotated as a salicylic acid-binding protein 2-like ( SABP2 ), has been identified in Arabidopsis for a role in powdery mildew resistance [ 34 ]. In our study, CmoCh03G010060 and CmoCh03G010010 did not show significant expression differences in the two squash genotypes from the start to 10 days post-inoculation. However, CmoCh03G010100, the SABP2-like gene, exhibited notable expression changes. Salicylic acid is crucial for the activation of defense genes in Arabidopsis [ 35 , 36 ], and high levels of SA are essential for activating local and systemic defense responses in cucumber and zucchini resistance to powdery mildew [ 37 , 38 ]. The expression of the SABP2-like gene is linked to the salicylic acid level, although it is unclear whether the Pm-0 resistance locus has been introgressed into the two genotypes in our research from previous breeding efforts. The significant downregulation of SABP2 -like gene expression at 6 h post-inoculation in the genotype SF02 might be related to powdery mildew susceptibility. An 11 bp insertion at the splice site region and two nonsynonymous mutations in the coding region of SF02 (as shown in Supplementary Figure S5 ) may result in a loss of function of this gene, thereby affecting SA expression. In contrast, the YD26 genotype maintains high levels of SA expression, enhancing resistance to powdery mildew through various defense mechanisms. This suggests that the high expression level of the SABP2-like gene might act as the causal gene in the Pm-0 locus, assuming the Pm-0 resistance locus was introgressed into at least one of the two genotypes. Alternatively, the observed improvement in powdery mildew resistance may be attributed to broad-spectrum resistance mediated by salicylic acid.
Powdery mildew resistance is considered a trait with a quantitative genetic basis in cucurbit plants [ 30 ]. In butternut squash, besides DEGs within the known resistance locus Pm-0 on chromosome 3, we identified a group of disease resistance gene analogs (RGAs) on chromosome 6 that showed significant expression differences between the two genotypes. This was determined through transcriptome data and qPCR expression analysis. These R gene analogs, which include genes with CC, NBS, and LRR domains, belong to the CNL class [ 39 ]. The disease resistance proteins recognize specific pathogen effectors and then activate a series of defense responses, including triggering signal transductions, activating hypersensitive responses (HRs), producing and releasing immune-related hormones [ 36 ]. In melon, candidate gene resistance to P. xanthii was found located in an RGA-rich region, and this region also conferred resistance to aphids and viruses [ 40 ]. Two nearby genes conferring resistance to three races of powdery mildew pathogen were identifies as NBS-LRR genes [ 41 ]. Although R gene-mediated disease resistance often exhibits race specificity, meaning that when pathogens mutate or evolve into new races, the R genes may no longer provide effective resistance, it is still evident that the immune response triggered by R genes represents a crucial defense mechanism for plants against pathogen infection.
Plant resistance genes have to evolve in response to selective pressure for resistance to pathogens [ 42 ]. NBS-LRR resistance genes have a clustered nature due to gene duplication and when the resistance genes are closely related and physically linked, which would promote more R gene conversion or recombination [ 43 , 44 , 45 ]. The well-known Mla locus of powdery mildew resistance in barley is associated with several NBS-LRR gene homologs [ 4 , 5 ]. The allelic variations in Mla are due to InDel and SNP mutations. In wheat, powdery mildew resistance alleles of Pm3 were found to evolve from the susceptible allele, and the mutations were all located in the LRR region [ 46 ]. In Cucumis melo , the Pm-w resistance locus, which confers high-level resistance to powdery mildew, was also found within a clustered NLRs region [ 47 , 48 ]. In our research, the high expression of RGAs transcripts in resistance genotype YD26 suggests the potential involvement of these LRR proteins in disease resistance to powdery mildew. This contrasts with the susceptible genotype SF02, where four frameshifts and two codon changes plus codon deletion within the R-gene cluster region ( Supplementary Figures S6 and S7 ) might lead to the lack of LRR protein expression. To further understand the role of these R genes, it will be necessary to identify the candidate locus from this region in an F2 population derived from the cross between YD26 and SF02.
As an obligate biotrophic pathogen, powdery mildew relies on the living cells and tissues of host plants to obtain nutrients for growth and reproduction. After the spores of powdery mildew germinate, hyphae are produced, which invade the epidermal cells, forming haustoria and secondary hyphae to absorb nutrients from the host cells, and then new spores are produced to complete their life cycle [ 1 ]. To prevent the attack from powdery mildew, plant R gene-mediated resistances occur when plant R proteins recognize pathogen effectors inside the host cell after a successful invasion. The mechanisms of S gene-mediated resistances underlying host–pathogen interactions in plants are different. The first known S gene is barley mlo , which was found early in the 1930s [ 13 ]. The MLO proteins have a specific seven-transmembrane (TM) domain [ 18 ], and the recessive mlo allele protein prevents spore penetration by forming cell wall appositions at the penetration site [ 16 ].
Research shows that MLO proteins exist in all plants, and the origin of MLO genes can be traced back at least to the early evolutionary stages of land plant development approximately 400–450 million years ago [ 49 ]. The requirement for MLO proteins of powdery mildews to enter plant cells has been conserved for at least 200 million years, at or before the monocot–dicot split [ 50 ], and diverse powdery mildews take advantage of MLO protein on membrane over time. Since the discovery of mlo -resistance in barley, powdery mildew resistance arising from MLO allele mutations has also been found in monocot wheat, as well as in dicot plants such as Arabidopsis , tomato, melon, cucumber, etc. [ 16 ]. In Arabidopsis , MLO negatively regulates PEN1-dependent secretion and results in an early failure of the penetration process of pathogens [ 51 ].
The S and R genes represent the different mechanisms underlying plant resistance to powdery mildew. R gene-related resistance is usually considered to be readily overcome by the evolution of pathogens, while the MLO resistance used in spring barley widely for decades provides the best evidence that S gene-related resistance is durable. These S genes that would provide durable resistance have their own primary genetic functions, so the loss of function may result in undesirable side effects, such as increased sensitivity to other stresses, dwarfing, or other negative consequences [ 12 ]. Barley MLO mutants show increased susceptibility to the rice blast fungus, accelerated leaf senescence, and reduced grain yield [ 14 ]. Although the MLO gene has been discovered in other crops, it has not been widely applied in commercial breeding as it has been in barley. In this study, despite the difference in powdery mildew resistance between the two squash varieties, the expression of the two MLO genes belonging to clade V in both varieties was not suppressed. Consequently, neither of them formed an effective physical barrier, allowing the powdery mildew pathogen to invade the pumpkin leaves further and trigger the subsequent expression of downstream R genes response.
Two squash genotypes, ‘YD26’ and ‘SF02’, were used in this research for powdery mildew inoculation. These genotypes were provided by the Vegetable Research Institute, Hainan Academy of Agricultural Sciences, and were identified through years of field observations in Hainan as resistant and susceptible to natural powdery mildew disease, respectively. Seeds of these genotypes were soaked in warm water at 50 °C to induce germination and then placed in a germination chamber. Once germinated and with developing roots, the seeds were transferred to Jiffy peat pellets and subsequently to 9 cm pots. The plantlets were grown in a chamber with a day/night temperature of 25/20 °C and a 16 h photoperiod.
Conidia of P. xanthii were collected directly from infected squash leaves and first inoculated onto the susceptible genotype ‘SF02’ to purify and propagate the pathogen. When seedlings of ‘YD26’ and ‘SF02’ had developed two true leaves, powdery mildew spores were collected and suspended in a freshly prepared solution of 0.5 × 10 6 spores/mL with Tween-20 for spray inoculation. Squash leaves surface-inoculated with powdery mildew were marked for sampling at 06, 12, 24, 36, and 48 h and 10 days (240 h) post-inoculation (hpi). Non-inoculated leaves (00 hpi) of both genotypes were used for whole-genome sequencing. Additionally, three leaves from both non-inoculated and inoculated treatments of the two squash genotypes were sampled for transcriptome sequencing. On day 10, infected leaves were evaluated for pathogen infection and scored on a scale from 0 (no infection) to 5 (completely infected).
Genomic DNA was extracted from young leaves of two-week-old seedlings of the ‘YD26’ and ‘SF02’ genotypes using the CTAB method. The concentration and quality of the total genomic DNA were assessed with a NanoDrop 2000 Spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and gel electrophoresis. DNA libraries with 350 bp fragments were prepared for Illumina/BGI sequencing, and sequencing was performed on an Illumina platform by Biomarker Technologies in Beijing, China, with 150 bp read lengths. Raw reads were processed using the BMKCloud online platform. During quality control, clean data were generated by removing reads with adapters, poly-N sequences, and low-quality reads. Metrics such as Q20, Q30, GC content, and sequence duplication levels were calculated from the clean data. The clean sequencing reads were then mapped to the reference C. moschata genome for variation analysis.
Two leaves of the squash genotypes ‘YD26’ and ‘SF02’ from each treatment were inserted in one tube and immediately submerged in liquid nitrogen. All samples were stored at −80 °C until used for transcriptome sequencing. The total RNA was extracted separately using the TIANGEN RNA kit following the manufacturer’s protocol. After checking and evaluating the quality, quantity, and integrity, RNA samples were used for transcriptome sequencing library preparation. The transcriptome sequencing library was constructed through RNA randomly fragmentation, cDNA strand 1/strand 2 synthesis, end repair, A-tailing, ligation of sequencing adapters, size selection, and library PCR enrichment, after which the library preparations were sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform and 150 bp paired-end reads were generated.
Raw reads in fastq format were processed and filtered to obtain the raw reads by moving the adapter and trimming the low-quality base. At the same time, Q20, Q30, and GC contents of the clean data were calculated. All the downstream analyses were based on the clean data with high quality. The C. moschata genome was used again, and the generated clean reads were mapped to the reference genome. Gene expression levels were quantified using Htseq-count, and FPKM values were calculated based on gene length and read counts, accounting for sequencing depth and gene length simultaneously. Gene Ontology (GO) and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses were conducted using the topGO and clusterProfiler R packages, respectively, to identify significantly enriched terms and pathways among differentially expressed genes.
To identify genes potentially induced by powdery mildew infection, we compared transcriptome data across various groups based on their expression patterns. The analysis focused on contrasting the non-treatment groups of the two squash genotypes, ‘YD26’ and ‘SF02’, with different time points post-infection against their respective non-treatment controls. For differential expression analysis, DESeq2 was employed for datasets with biological replicates, while edgeR was used for datasets lacking biological replicates. Statistical significance was determined with a threshold of 0.05, and p -values were adjusted for multiple comparisons using the Benjamini and Hochberg method to control the false discovery rate. MLO protein sequences from Arabidopsis , cucumber, and monostylous crops (barley, rice, etc.) were obtained from NCBI aa. Blasting these MLO sequences from the public database with our butter squash sequencing data, twenty C. moschata MLO (short as CmMLO ) sequences were identified and named CmMLO1 to CmMLO20 , respectively, based on the location on the chromosome of C. moschata . A phylogenetic tree was constructed by MEGA 7.0.26 with the maximum likelihood method and 1000 bootstrap replications using all the MLO protein sequences from Arabidopsis , cucumber, and monocotylous crops.
Two leaves from infected squash seedlings were sampled for total RNA extraction. Three biological replicates were used for each treatment, and the same samples were employed for RNA-seq. RNA was extracted using Trizol (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) following the manufacturer’s protocol. The quality and quantity of RNA samples were assessed using a 1% agarose gel and a NanoDrop spectrophotometer. Following DNase treatment to remove genomic DNA, 1 µg of RNA was used for cDNA synthesis using the iScript™ cDNA Synthesis Kit (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). For quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR), a 10 µL reaction mix was prepared, consisting of 2 µL cDNA template (~50 ng/µL), 5 µL 2× iQ™ SYBR ® Green Supermix (Bio-Rad, CA, US), 0.3 µL each of forward and reverse primers (10 µM), and 2.7 µL Milli-Q water. The qRT-PCR was conducted with an initial denaturation step at 95 °C for 3 min, followed by 40 cycles of 15 s at 95 °C and 1 min at 60 °C. A final melting curve was generated by holding at 95 °C for 10 s, then at 65 °C for 5 s, with a gradual increase to 95 °C at 0.5 °C increments. ACTIN was used as the reference gene for normalization, and the primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S6 .
