Different immune elicitor treatments had significant effects on the dynamic changes of 6 endogenous hormones (IAA, TZR, SA, JA, ABA, GA 3 ) in tomato leaves, with the following response patterns ( Figures 2A–F ):
Hormone contents in tomato leaves after different immune elicitor treatments (A–F) is IAA, TZR, SA, JA, ABA, and GA 3 content, respectively. Different lowercase letters after data in the same column indicate significant differences (P < 0.05).
Indole-3-acetic acid ( Figure 2A ): The clean water control group showed a “slow decrease - slow increase” trend in IAA content, with the 4th sampling close to the initial value. The 5% amino-oligosaccharin (A) and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein (B) treatment groups showed a “slow increase - slow decrease - significant recovery” trend in IAA content, with the 4th sampling about 5 ng/g higher than the initial value. The 5% S-ABA (C) treatment group showed the same trend as the control. The Kang’erjian Plant Vaccine (D) treatment group showed a “decrease - rapid increase” trend in IAA content, about 10 ng/g higher than the initial value. As a plant growth-promoting hormone, increased IAA content can promote tomato plant vegetative growth, laying a material foundation for disease resistance, indicating that A, B, and D treatments have positive regulatory effects on plant growth.
Trans-zeatin riboside ( Figure 2B ): The A, B treatment groups and control group all showed continuous upward trends in TZR content, with the 4th sampling increasing by 6 ng/g, 10 ng/g, and 2 ng/g respectively compared to initial values. The C and D treatment groups showed no significant changes in TZR content, with final values basically equal to initial values. TZR can promote cell division and robust plant growth. The enhancing effects of A and B treatments indicate that they can strengthen tomato plant vegetative growth potential and improve disease resistance capacity.
Salicylic acid ( Figure 2C ): All treatment groups showed “increase - decrease - re-increase” fluctuation trends in SA content, with A and B treatment groups showing the most significant enhancement effects, increasing by about 200 ng/g at the 4th sampling compared to initial values. The D treatment group increased by about 50 ng/g, while the C group and control group showed no significant enhancement. SA is the core signaling substance of plant systemic acquired resistance, capable of directly activating plant disease defense pathways. The significant induction effects of A and B treatments on SA are important mechanisms for their enhancement of TYLCV resistance.
Jasmonic acid ( Figure 2D ): All treatment groups showed continuous downward trends in JA content, with A and B treatment groups showing the smallest decrease amplitudes of 422.69 ng/g and 295.65 ng/g respectively. The D treatment group and control group showed the largest decrease amplitudes of 763.30 ng/g and 753.77 ng/g respectively. Tomato JA content abnormally increases after TYLCV inoculation, thereby inhibiting plant growth. A and B treatments can significantly reduce the decrease rate of JA, effectively alleviating the growth inhibition effect of virus on plants.
Abscisic acid ( Figure 2E ): All treatment groups showed “first increase - then decrease - tend to flatten” trends in ABA content, with A, B, D treatment groups and control group showing relatively small overall changes. However, the C treatment group showed a rapid increase in ABA content at the 2nd sampling and a sharp decrease at the 3rd sampling, with significant fluctuation amplitude. As a growth-inhibiting hormone, TYLCV infection leads to increased ABA content. Various immune elicitor treatments can reduce ABA accumulation to different degrees, alleviating virus-induced growth inhibition.
Gibberellin ( Figure 2F ): All treatment groups showed “decrease - increase - tend to flatten” trends in GA 3 content, with A, B, D treatment groups showing higher GA 3 content at initial stage. By the 4th sampling, there were no significant differences in GA 3 content among the 5 treatment groups. As an important growth-promoting hormone, there were no significant differences in final GA 3 content among treatments in this experiment, indicating that different immune elicitors have no significant differential regulatory effects on tomato GA 3 metabolism.
Comprehensive evaluation of the regulatory effects on 6 endogenous hormones: 5% amino-oligosaccharin (A) and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein (B) can significantly optimize tomato hormone balance, increase growth-promoting hormones and disease resistance signal hormones, reduce growth-inhibiting hormone levels, and show significantly better therapeutic effects on tomato yellow leaf curl virus disease than other treatments.
Peroxidase (POD), catalase (CAT), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) are core defense enzyme systems in plants for scavenging reactive oxygen species and resisting stress. Peroxidase ( Figure 3A ): At initial sampling, A, B, and D treatment groups showed significantly higher POD activity than C group and control group, subsequently showing “decrease - increase” trends. The control group showed a continuous upward trend in POD activity. By the 4th sampling, POD activities of the 5 treatment groups tended to be similar. As a key enzyme in plant stress response, POD can catalyze reactive oxygen species decomposition. The high initial POD activity of A and B treatments indicates that they can rapidly activate tomato stress defense responses.
Catalase ( Figure 3B ): At initial sampling, B, C, and A treatment groups showed higher CAT activity. CAT activities of all treatment groups gradually became consistent with sampling time progression, with no significant differences at the 4th sampling. CAT synergizes with POD to scavenge hydrogen peroxide. The early enhancement of its activity indicates that A and B treatments can rapidly initiate the plant’s reactive oxygen species scavenging system.
Superoxide dismutase ( Figure 3C ): At initial sampling, there were no significant differences in SOD activity among the 5 treatment groups. With experiment progression, except for the A treatment group where enzyme activity recovered at the 4th sampling, other treatment groups all showed downward trends, with no significant differences among treatment groups throughout. As the first line of defense for reactive oxygen species scavenging, the lack of significant differences in SOD activity in this experiment indicates that different immune elicitors have relatively weak regulatory effects on tomato SOD metabolism.
Comprehensive evaluation of activity changes in 3 defense enzymes: 5% amino-oligosaccharin (A) and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein (B) can significantly increase activities of key defense enzymes such as POD and CAT at early treatment stages, rapidly activate the plant’s antioxidant defense system, enhance tomato resistance response to TYLCV, and are superior elicitors for regulating tomato defense enzyme systems.
Combining the regulatory effects of different immune elicitors on tomato leaf endogenous hormone contents and defense enzyme activities, 5% amino-oligosaccharin aqueous solution and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein wettable powder can significantly optimize tomato hormone metabolism balance, rapidly activate plant defense enzyme systems, effectively enhance tomato resistance to yellow leaf curl virus disease, and are high-efficiency plant immune elicitors screened in this experiment, providing material basis for subsequent control effect experiments.
There were significant differences among different chemical treatments in delaying the disease progression of tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) and controlling its disease index ( Tables 1 , 2 ). The results showed that on September 28 (after two sprays of the agents), only the clean water control group developed infected plants, with a disease index of 0.10, while no disease was observed in any of the other treatments, indicating that all tested agents effectively delayed the initial onset of TYLCV. On October 8 (after three sprays), infected plants appeared in all treatments. The control group had the highest disease index (0.22), while the disease indices of T1, T2, T3, and T4 were 0.10, 0.15, 0.05, and 0.10, respectively. From October 18 to November 8, the number of infected plants continued to increase across all treatments. The control group consistently exhibited the highest disease index, whereas the treated groups showed a significantly slower disease progression rate. Among them, T3 (combination of 5% amino-oligosaccharin + 6% oligosaccharin·chain protein) maintained the lowest disease index throughout. At the end of the experiment (November 8), the disease index of T3 was 0.25, which was lower than that of T1 (5% amino-oligosaccharin alone), T2 (6% oligosaccharin·chain protein alone), and T4 (chemical agent moroxydine-copper acetate). The control efficacy of T3 against TYLCV reached 70.93%.

According to the conversion relationship between CT values and viral copy numbers, the viral load of the combined treatment group was approximately 7.8 × 10^5 copies/μL, while that of the chemical agent moroxydine hydrochloride-copper treatment group was as high as 4.9 × 10^6 copies/μL, a difference of more than 6 times. The results fully demonstrate that combined use of 5% amino-oligosaccharin and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein can significantly inhibit TYLCV proliferation in tomato plants and is the optimal agent combination for TYLCV control.
Plant resistance to viral diseases results from the coordinated action of various physiological processes including endogenous hormone metabolism and defense enzyme system activation. The present study specifically targeted monopartite TYLCV, which is the predominant form causing epidemics in Chinese tomato production systems ( Czosnek and Laterrot, 1997 ; Moriones and Navas-Castillo, 2000 ). This study found that 5% amino-oligosaccharin and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein can enhance tomato resistance to TYLCV through dual pathways of hormone regulation and defense enzyme activation, consistent with previous research results on immune elicitors controlling plant viral diseases ( Su et al., 2004 ; Sun et al., 2014 ; Wang et al., 2020 ).
Hormonal signaling integration and redox crosstalk. The observed changes in SA, JA, and ABA suggest complex regulatory interactions that are central to plant immune responses. Recent studies have highlighted the intricate crosstalk between these hormones and reactive oxygen species (ROS) in orchestrating plant defense networks ( Ali et al., 2025b ; Parveen et al., 2022 ). Salicylic acid, as the core signaling molecule of plant systemic acquired resistance, can activate expression of downstream disease resistance-related genes and induce broad-spectrum disease resistance in plants ( Li et al., 2010 ; Yan et al., 2018 ). In this experiment, 5% amino-oligosaccharin and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein treatments could significantly increase SA content in tomato leaves, indicating that they can enhance tomato systemic acquired resistance to TYLCV by activating SA-mediated disease resistance signaling pathways. This aligns with research demonstrating that SA-mediated defense responses are modulated by cellular redox status, with low ascorbate abundance triggering changes in hormone sensitivity that steer adaptive plant responses toward SA defenses ( Foyer et al., 2012 ).
The integration of hormone and redox signaling is further evidenced by the JA and ABA dynamics observed in this study. While SA typically antagonizes JA-dependent defenses to prioritize SA-dependent resistance, this regulatory framework is profoundly influenced by ROS-mediated signaling networks ( Ali et al., 2025b ; Parveen et al., 2022 ). The ability of amino-oligosaccharin and oligosaccharin-chain protein treatments to significantly reduce JA decrease rates while maintaining ABA homeostasis suggests that these elicitors activate a coordinated hormonal-redox response that optimizes the balance between growth and defense.
Auxin-driven resilience pathways. Notably, this study demonstrated that both elicitors significantly increased IAA content, providing evidence for the involvement of auxin-driven resilience pathways in TYLCV resistance. Recent comprehensive reviews have established that auxins play multifaceted roles in enabling plants to cope with environmental stresses by regulating growth and activating defense mechanisms. The TIR1/AFB-Aux/IAA-ARF signaling cascade, central to auxin perception, has been shown to interact extensively with stress-responsive pathways, including those mediated by SA, JA, and ABA. Specifically, auxin signaling can enhance resistance against viral infections by inducing the transcription of specific defense-related genes ( Ali et al., 2025b ).
The crosstalk between auxin and ROS is particularly relevant to the observed enhancement of POD and CAT activities in this study. Research has demonstrated that auxin homeostasis in specific tissues is crucial for regulating H 2 O 2 production through altered expression of antioxidant enzymes. The auxin signaling mutant tir1afb2 exhibits reduced accumulation of H 2 O 2 and superoxide anion, alongside enhanced activities of catalase and ascorbate peroxidase, indicating that optimal auxin signaling is required for precise ROS modulation during stress responses ( Tognetti et al., 2011 ). The elevated IAA levels observed in amino-oligosaccharin and oligosaccharin-chain protein treated plants likely contribute to the enhanced POD and CAT activities through auxin-ROS crosstalk, thereby establishing a robust antioxidant defense system against TYLCV-induced oxidative stress.
Antioxidant enzyme activation and ROS homeostasis. In terms of defense enzyme systems, peroxidase and catalase are key enzymes for scavenging reactive oxygen species in plants. Viral infection leads to massive accumulation of reactive oxygen species in plants, causing cellular oxidative damage, while defense enzyme system activation can effectively scavenge reactive oxygen species and alleviate oxidative stress ( Zhang et al., 2024 ). In this experiment, 5% amino-oligosaccharin and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein could significantly increase POD and CAT activities at early treatment stages, rapidly initiate plant antioxidant defense responses, and reduce cellular damage caused by TYLCV infection.
The rapid activation of POD and CAT observed in this study aligns with recent advances in understanding ROS-mediated defense networks. ROS, including superoxide anion, hydrogen peroxide, and hydroxyl radicals, are generated through various enzymatic pathways and serve dual functions: inhibiting pathogen growth while activating defense-related gene expression as signaling molecules. The oxidative burst triggered by pathogen recognition initiates hypersensitive response and facilitates the establishment of systemic acquired resistance by inducing systemic signaling networks. The interplay between ROS and phytohormones such as JA, SA, and auxin further complicates this regulatory framework, underscoring the importance of coordinated hormonal-redox signaling in orchestrating both local and systemic defense responses ( Ali et al., 2025a ). The lack of significant differences in superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity among treatments suggests that SOD may not be a core enzyme in tomato TYLCV defense response, or that elicitor regulatory effects on it have time- or concentration-dependent characteristics requiring further experimental verification.
Comprehensive hormonal balance optimization. Meanwhile, the two elicitors could significantly increase IAA and TZR contents, reduce levels of growth-inhibiting hormones such as jasmonic acid and abscisic acid, optimize tomato endogenous hormone balance, and promote plant vegetative growth. As an important growth-promoting hormone, GA 3 showed no significant differences in final content among treatments, indicating it is not a key hormone for the two elicitors to regulate ( Ali et al., 2025a ) tomato TYLCV resistance, providing direction for subsequent in-depth research on elicitor action targets.
This study found that combined use of 5% amino-oligosaccharin and 6% oligosaccharin-chain protein showed significantly better control effects on tomato TYLCV than single treatments, manifested as the fewest diseased plants and lowest viral load, showing obvious synergistic enhancement effects.
Dual-receptor recognition and signal amplification. Amino-oligosaccharin, a deacetylation product of chitin, can be recognized by pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) on the plant cell membrane. Studies have shown that in tomato, Bti9 (also known as SlLYK13 ), a homolog of chitin elicitor receptor kinase 1 ( CERK1 ), is a key component of chitin signaling, responsible for recognizing chitin oligosaccharides and triggering downstream immune responses. Amino-oligosaccharin activates plant pattern-triggered immunity (PTI) by binding to CERK1, leading to a burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS), calcium influx, and activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cascade ( Sun et al., 2025 ). Oligosaccharin·chain protein consists of oligosaccharide fragments and a disease resistance protein; the resistance protein component may be recognized by plants through a receptor system different from that for amino-oligosaccharin. Proteinaceous elicitors typically initiate calcium signaling and ROS production via receptor kinases or direct action on the lipid bilayer of the cell membrane ( Popa et al., 2026 ). Thus, the two elicitors may simultaneously activate plant immune perception through distinct receptor systems, producing a “dual-receptor recognition” effect that amplifies the initial input of immune signals.
Enhanced MAPK signaling and transcriptional regulation. Studies indicate that the synergistic action of different elicitors can alter MAPK phosphorylation dynamics and enhance immune responses. The combination of amino-oligosaccharin and oligosaccharin-chain protein may simultaneously activate multiple MAPK cascades, thereby achieving a superposition of signaling pathways. Specifically, amino-oligosaccharin primarily signals through the CERK1-RLCK-MAPK3/6 pathway, whereas oligosaccharin-chain protein may enhance signal transduction through additional MAPK modules. Their synergy can form a stronger immune response network ( Greco et al., 2025 ).
The integration of these signaling pathways likely converges on WRKY transcription factors, which serve as central nodes in the hormonal-redox signaling network. WRKY TFs mediate PTI cascades downstream of MAPK signaling and are modulators of plant tolerance to biotic stress and systemic acquired resistance ( Zhang et al., 2025 ). These TFs adjust ET, JA, and SA interactive pathways, and control developmental processes through cytokinin and auxin, thereby coordinating the complex defense response required for TYLCV resistance.
Strengthened SA signaling through parallel pathways. Salicylic acid (SA) is a core signaling molecule in plant systemic acquired resistance (SAR). In this study, single and combined treatments of amino-oligosaccharin and oligosaccharin·chain protein all significantly increased SA content in tomato leaves. Research has shown that the antiviral resistance induced by amino-oligosaccharin primarily depends on the SA-mediated signaling pathway, characterized by upregulation of the pathogenesis-related protein 1 (PR1) gene ( Jia et al., 2016 ). Oligosaccharin·chain protein may enhance SA signaling through additional mechanisms. Proteinaceous elicitors can induce activation of calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs), which then phosphorylate and activate WRKY transcription factors, forming an SA signal amplification loop parallel to NPR1 ( Sun et al., 2025 ). Therefore, the combined treatment may strengthen SA signal transduction through both NPR1-dependent and WRKY-dependent mechanisms, achieving a “signal pathway superposition” effect.
The superior performance of the combined elicitor treatment over chemical agents can be attributed to its ability to activate multiple layers of plant immunity while maintaining hormonal and redox homeostasis. The chemical agent moroxydine-copper acetate, while providing some antiviral effect, does not induce the comprehensive systemic resistance and sustained antioxidant defense observed with the elicitor combination. This highlights the advantage of plant immune inducers in engaging natural defense networks that provide broad-spectrum, long-lasting protection against viral diseases.
The green development of the tomato industry requires reducing the use of chemical pesticides and promoting environmentally friendly disease control technologies. Plant immune inducers, owing to their advantages of no residues, low risk of resistance development, and ability to improve crop quality, have become ideal agents for the green control of tomato TYLCV ( Wang et al., 2025b ). Both 5% amino-oligosaccharin and 6% oligosaccharin·chain protein screened in this study are bio-sourced inducers. Their combined application can significantly reduce the incidence of TYLCV in autumn tomato cultivation, and the method is simple (foliar spray, three consecutive applications), making it suitable for promotion and adoption by farmers.
Currently, the application of plant immune inducers still faces some challenges, such as their efficacy being greatly influenced by crop variety, growth stage, environmental conditions, etc., and the induced resistance having a certain duration ( Yu et al., 2013 ). In the future, this inducer combination can be integrated with biological control measures (e.g., releasing the whitefly natural enemy Encarsia formosa) to build a more efficient and environmentally friendly integrated control system for tomato TYLCV, promoting high-quality and sustainable development of the tomato industry.
This study only used the tomato variety “Nongbo Pink 18109” as experimental material, and the applicability of its results to other tomato varieties still requires verification. Based on the current findings, it is plausible that the elicitor combination may exhibit differential effects depending on the variety’s baseline susceptibility to TYLCV. For highly susceptible varieties, the induced resistance might be more noticeable due to a stronger contrast with untreated controls, whereas moderately resistant or tolerant varieties may show a more limited incremental benefit, as they already possess partial defense mechanisms. Conversely, varieties with inherent resistance could potentially respond more robustly to immune inducers if their genetic background facilitates signal amplification. Therefore, further studies across a range of tomato genotypes with varying TYLCV susceptibility levels are needed to delineate the variety-specific efficacy of this elicitor combination.
Meanwhile, experiments were only conducted under greenhouse conditions with insect-proof nets. Although nets were installed, whitefly penetration still occurred, contributing to virus spread. In open-field environments, whitefly pressure is typically much higher due to unrestricted pest movement, larger population sizes, and less controlled microclimates. Under such conditions, the efficacy of foliar-applied immune inducers alone may be compromised, as continuous virus inoculation from immigrating whiteflies can overwhelm induced resistance. Consequently, the application strategy should be adjusted. Integration with systemic insecticides is likely necessary to reduce vector population and virus transmission at the source. Additionally, more frequent or higher-concentration applications of the elicitor combination might be required to maintain elevated defense levels. A practical integrated approach could combine the elicitor spray schedule with timely insecticide applications, reinforced physical barriers (e.g., high-density nets or insect-proof screens), and cultural practices such as reflective mulches or trap crops. Further field trials are essential to optimize this integrated strategy under real-world, high-whitefly-pressure conditions.
Future research can be expanded from the following aspects: ① Conduct elicitor control effect experiments across different tomato varieties and cultivation modes to refine technical parameters; ② Explore the combined application of elicitors with biological pesticides, physical insect prevention measures, and systemic insecticides to develop comprehensive integrated pest management (IPM) protocols;③ Analyze the molecular mechanisms by which the combination of amino-oligosaccharin and oligosaccharin-chain protein regulates tomato resistance to TYLCV, with particular focus on the integration of hormone signaling, ROS homeostasis, and defense gene activation, providing a theoretical basis for the efficient utilization of immune inducers.

title: Dissecting heterosis and combining ability for yield and TYLCV resistance in tomato under field conditions
text:
Tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum L.) is one of the most important horticultural crops worldwide, with yield and fruit quality strongly constrained by biotic stresses, particularly tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV). Hybrid breeding through the exploitation of heterosis is a highly effective approach for improving yield, fruit quality, and TYLCV resistance. To investigate the genetic basis of heterosis and trait inheritance, 17 determinate female and 7 semi-determinate male inbred lines were crossed in a North Carolina Design II (NCII) scheme, generating 119 F₁ hybrids evaluated alongside their parents and control cultivars. To ensure uniform and consistent TYLCV infection pressure, the highly susceptible cultivar ‘Matin’ was interplanted throughout the field as a spreader genotype.
Heterosis analysis revealed substantial positive better-parent heterosis (BPH) for yield-related traits, particularly single-plant yield and fruit number per plant, whereas negative heterosis was favorable for traits such as sunscald incidence, fruit acidity, and TYLCV severity. Genetic variance partitioning indicated that reproductive traits such as number of inflorescences on the main stem (NIMS), number of flowers per inflorescence (NFI), and number of fruits per inflorescence (NFPI) were predominantly governed by additive effects, suggesting that parental selection can efficiently improve these traits. In contrast, TYLCV resistance was strongly influenced by non-additive variance, highlighting the critical role of specific combining ability and hybrid interactions. Several hybrids combined high yield with complete resistance to TYLCV, underscoring the potential for simultaneous improvement of productivity and resilience.
This study not only clarifies the genetic basis of heterosis in tomato but also identifies elite parental lines and superior hybrids that can serve as valuable resources for breeding programs aimed at developing resilient, high-yielding cultivars under biotic and climatic stress conditions.
The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12870-026-08806-1.
Tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum L.) stands among the most economically and nutritionally significant horticultural crops worldwide. Its widespread cultivation spanning over 5.4 million hectares globally reflects its central role in both subsistence and commercial agriculture. Iran, with approximately 77,000 hectares dedicated to tomato farming, an annual output surpassing 3.4 million tons, and an average yield of 45 tons per hectare (well above the global average of 38 tons per hectare), currently ranks as the 11th largest tomato producer globally [ 1 ].
One of the most effective breeding approaches for enhancing yield, fruit quality, and TYLCV resistance in tomato is the development of F₁ hybrids through the exploitation of heterosis, or hybrid vigor. Heterosis, a genetic phenomenon primarily expressed in the F₁ generation, tends to increase with greater genetic divergence between parental lines but typically diminishes in subsequent generations [ 2 ]. The effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated by its widespread implementation in crops such as rapeseed, rice, and cotton, where hybrid cultivars account for over 90%, 70%, and 80% of total production, respectively [ 2 ]. Numerous studies have reported yield and quality enhancements of up to 60% in F₁ hybrids relative to their parental lines, with notable improvements in fruit uniformity, TYLCV resistance, and post-harvest shelf life [ 3 , 4 ]. In tomato, hybrid combinations involving phenotypically divergent parents particularly with respect to plant architecture and growth dynamics have exhibited significantly improved yields, largely due to favorable interactions during both vegetative and reproductive growth phases [ 5 ]. These advantages were primarily attributed to synergistic effects on key traits such as flower number, fruit weight, and soluble solids content. It has been shown that crosses between vigorous, well-balanced parental lines resulted in the highest levels of heterosis.
To identify elite parents and hybrid combinations with superior performance, a comprehensive genetic dissection involving general combining ability (GCA) and specific combining ability (SCA) is necessary. GCA reflects additive genetic variance and is instrumental in evaluating parental line performance, while SCA captures non-additive effects, including dominance and epistasis, and is closely linked to hybrid performance [ 6 , 7 ]. Although several studies, including Xiang et al. [ 8 ], have noted correlations between parental traits and GCA estimates, these metrics alone often fall short in accurately predicting heterosis levels. As such, robust statistical mating designs such as North Carolina Design II (NCII) or the Griffing method are indispensable tools for partitioning genetic variance and accurately estimating both GCA and SCA [ 9 ].
Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), a member of the Geminiviridae family and Begomovirus genus, is one of the most economically destructive pathogens affecting Solanum lycopersicum cultivation globally, especially in major tomato-producing countries such as China, Italy, Egypt, Iran, and the United States [ 1 , 10 ]. While TYLCV can be transmitted through seeds [ 11 – 13 ], its primary vector is the whitefly, Bemisia tabaci , whose population density significantly correlates with TYLCV outbreaks [ 14 ]. Infected plants exhibit symptoms such as severe stunting, chlorosis, leaf curling, flower drop, and reduced fruit quality [ 15 , 16 ]. Notably, B. tabaci thrives in high-temperature environments, further exacerbating TYLCV spread in warm climates [ 17 ]. Integrated management relies on host resistance, quarantine of infected material, and vector control [ 18 ].
Given the mounting challenges of climate change, including increased temperatures and intensified outbreaks of TYLCV, the development of resistant, high-yielding tomato hybrids has become an urgent breeding priority particularly in regions like Iran where agroclimatic conditions strongly favor virus proliferation [ 19 , 20 ]. Numerous studies have established a direct link between rising temperatures, expanding B. tabaci populations, and the geographic and epidemiological spread of TYLCV [ 17 ]. Climate projection models further predict the intensification of this issue under future scenarios, underscoring the importance of breeding strategies that emphasize both durable resistance and climate adaptability [ 21 ]. The market value of tomato hybrids with TYLCV resistance is not comparable to that of susceptible hybrids, and most farmers avoid cultivating susceptible varieties.
Building upon the theoretical framework proposed by Krieger et al. [ 5 ], who identified the SINGLE FLOWER TRUSS (SFT) gene as a key determinant of heterosis in tomato, parental lines in this study were deliberately selected based on contrasting determinate and semi-determinate growth habits and vegetative vigor to align with the dosage-dependent overdominance model underlying yield heterosis. Krieger et al. [ 5 ] demonstrated that heterozygosity at the SFT locus can increase fruit yield by up to 60% through a dosage-dependent balance between flowering and vegetative growth. This finding provided the first direct evidence of single-gene overdominance for yield in crops and underpins the objectives of the present study.
Although a considerable body of research has investigated TYLCV resistance genes, claimed resistant genotypes should be evaluated under natural field conditions with uniform virus pressure. All hybrids and lines were evaluated in a farm with uniform incidence of TYLCV. A very susceptible genotype (Matin) was cultivated in different parts of the farm to spread the TYLCV uniformly across the lines and hybrids which were cultivated for resistance evaluation. Finding the most resistant hybrids was the main purpose of this research. However, the next aim was to evaluate the heritability of important traits in tomato. This study thus aimed to conduct an in-depth genetic analysis of heterosis, variance components, heritability, and combining abilities for 18 agronomic and quality-related traits. In addition, genetic parameters of four key reproductive traits including the number of inflorescences per plant, the number of flowers per inflorescence, the number of fruits per inflorescence, and resistance to TYLCV were evaluated using the NCII crossing scheme. The overarching goal was to identify high-performing parental inbred lines and F₁ hybrid combinations that exhibit superior agronomic performance, resilience under climate stress, and stable pathogen resistance, thereby contributing to the development of elite commercial hybrids in the face of ongoing climatic and biological challenges.
In this study, a total of 24 selected parental inbred lines (F₆), including 17 female and 7 male lines, were used to analyze combining ability and heterosis in tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum L.). These lines were derived from six generations of selfing and selection, developed as part of a breeding program conducted at two experimental stations affiliated with the University of Tehran. Specifically, the inbred lines have been continuously developed, selected, and evaluated over the past ten years at the College of Abouraihan, University of Tehran, as part of a long-term tomato breeding program. In addition to differences in growth habit and plant architecture, the parental inbred lines were selected based on their contrasting phenotypic performance for key agronomic and stress-related traits. An initial population of 650 tomato inbred lines was developed using the single-seed descent (SSD) method and evaluated under field conditions across two contrasting environments. Pakdasht, characterized by high natural pressure of whiteflies and TYLCV, was used to assess virus response, while Karaj provided favorable conditions for evaluating yield and agronomic performance. During the first screening cycle, eight plants per line were evaluated for TYLCV severity under natural infection in Pakdasht, and the same lines were assessed for yield-related traits in Karaj. Lines exhibiting a TYLCV severity score greater than 3 on a 0–5 scale were eliminated regardless of yield performance. Through this dual-environment phenotypic screening, 50 lines were selected from the initial population. These lines were subsequently cultivated in greenhouse for hybrid development. At the greenhouse due to high infestation of whitefly, TYLCV symptoms were observed during plant growth. This was another chance to detect susceptible lines and led to further elimination of TYLCV-susceptible inbred lines. Ultimately, 24 parental inbred lines (17 female and 7 male) were retained, each having undergone at least two independent phenotypic screenings for TYLCV tolerance and agronomic suitability. These materials are not publicly registered in germplasm databases and therefore do not have assigned accession numbers. The classification of male and female parental lines was carried out based on contrasting phenotypic traits in vegetative growth and plant architecture, to maximize heterosis effects in line with the theoretical framework proposed by Krieger et al. [ 5 ]. However, the parental lines were selected based on phenotypic performance and breeding relevance rather than prior molecular characterization of flowering-related loci. Therefore, interpretations related to the SFT locus in this study are grounded in established theoretical models and observed phenotypic outcomes, rather than direct genotypic confirmation.
In November 2022, controlled crosses were performed following the North Carolina Design II (NCII), using 17 female lines (determinate growth type) and 7 male lines (semi-determinate or vegetative growth type) in the Golfam greenhouse complex (Pakdasht, Iran). Parental seeds were sown in seedling trays filled with a cocopeat–perlite substrate, and seedlings were transplanted to greenhouse beds after the emergence of the second true leaf. Greenhouse conditions were maintained at a temperature of 24–26 °C during the day and 18–20 °C at night, with relative humidity ranging from 45 to 55%. Plants were grown under natural daylight conditions. For hybridization, as female flowers mature earlier than male flowers, female buds were emasculated 2–3 days before anticipated anthesis. Flowers were selected when the petals were white. Emasculation was performed during the day time using sterilized forceps. Next day in the morning (around 9 o’clock) pollen from fully opened male flowers was collected into microtubes and then manually applied to the stigmas of the emasculated female flowers. Pollinated flowers were labeled, and, when necessary, excess flowers on the same inflorescence were removed to ensure accurate crossing. Approximately 10 flowers were pollinated per each planned cross to achieve a minimum of 5–6 successful fruit sets. Each line was grown with multiple plants (10 plants per inbred line) to maximize the chance of successful hybridization. The overall success rate of crosses was approximately 60%. Mature fruits were harvested at full physiological ripeness, and seeds were extracted via fermentation, followed by washing and drying. A total of 119 hybrids (7♂ × 17♀) were successfully obtained. The contrasting parental lines (determinate × semi-determinate) provided an opportunity to evaluate heterosis expression in relation to vegetative reproductive trade-offs, similar to the model proposed for SFT heterozygotes [ 5 ].
In 2023 summer growing season, a total of 1,304 individual plants, including 24 parental inbred lines, 119 F₁ hybrids, and four commercial control cultivars (Bedero, Brivio, 8320, and Matin), were evaluated at two research stations located in Karaj and Pakdasht. For each genotype, eight plants were grown per plot. According to the augmented design, only the four commercial control cultivars were replicated within each station. Each control cultivar was included once in each of the five blocks per station, resulting in a total of 20 observations (4 control cultivars × 5 blocks) per station. In contrast, the parental inbred lines and F₁ hybrids were evaluated without replication.
Seeds were sown in seedling trays containing a cocopeat–perlite mixture, and the seedlings were transplanted to the field at the 2–3 leaf stage. Row spacing was set at 1.5 m, with 40 cm between plants. The Karaj station, with favorable environmental conditions and fertile soil, was used to evaluate fruit yield and quality traits, whereas the Pakdasht station, characterized by higher temperatures and a natural population of whiteflies (vectors of TYLCV), was used to screen for resistance to TYLCV. To ensure uniform natural infection pressure, the highly susceptible cultivar “Matin” was planted throughout the entire field and among all plots, allowing for widespread and homogeneous virus spread (Supplementary Fig. S3). This natural field setup also provided the basis to test whether heterosis for yield and resistance could be partly explained by the same overdominant mechanisms identified for the SFT locus, particularly through enhanced reproductive performance under stress conditions [ 5 ].
Resistance to TYLCV was evaluated individually in all 1,304 single plants (eight plants per genotype were evaluated individually, and the scores were averaged). All 119 F₁ hybrids were included in combining ability and genetic variance analyses for TYLCV score, as complete datasets were available for these traits across all hybrids. TYLCV symptoms were recorded using a standard 0–5 scale (22): (0) No symptoms; (1) Leaf yellowing, size reduction, and mild downward curling; (2) Leaf thickening, pronounced downward curling, and internode shortening; (3) Severe curling and abnormal stem growth; (4) Severe wrinkling, stunting, and edge cupping; (5) Extreme stunting and total yield loss. Each genotype was scored at the peak of whitefly infestation, 60 days after transplanting (DAT), when plants had fruits at the onset of ripening stage and disease symptoms were fully expressed. The mean TYLCV score of the eight plants per genotype was calculated and treated as a continuous variable for subsequent combining ability, heterosis, and variance component analyses, which is a common practice in quantitative genetic studies of disease resistance.
Following field establishment, a two-stage evaluation strategy was implemented. All 119 F₁ hybrids were included in combining ability and genetic variance analyses for three reproductive traits, including the number of inflorescences on the main stem (NIMS), number of flowers per inflorescence (NFI), and number of fruits per inflorescence (NFPI), as complete datasets were available for these traits across all hybrids. These reproductive traits were emphasized because they represent key components of yield heterosis in tomato, as previously shown by Krieger et al. [ 5 ], who linked SFT heterozygosity to increased inflorescence and flower production. Subsequently, a subset of 51 F₁ hybrids was selected for heterosis analysis and detailed evaluation of 18 agronomic and fruit quality traits. This selection was based on preliminary field-based ranked assessments conducted by three experienced tomato breeding specialists. Selection criteria included plant vigor and health, canopy coverage related to sunscald tolerance, fruit firmness, fruit shape and marketability, and overall yield potential. Traits were ranked using an ordinal scoring system (1 = poor, 2 = intermediate, 3 = desirable), and only hybrids with high agronomic relevance and average ranking scores above the predefined threshold (2.5) were retained for further laboratory and field evaluations.
Agronomic and fruit quality traits were evaluated in Karaj under open-field conditions. Single-plant yield (SPY, kg/plant), fruit number per plant (FNPP), and single fruit weight (SFW, g) were determined based on cumulative data from three consecutive harvests, as fruits did not ripen simultaneously. The maturity dates of the genotypes varied, ranging from 107 to 136 days after transplanting (DAT). At each harvest, all marketable fruits (full physiological maturity) from all eight plants were collected and their total number and total weight were recorded for each genotype. SPY was calculated as the total fruit weight divided by the number of remaining healthy plants. FNPP was calculated by dividing the total number of fruits by the number of remaining healthy plants. SFW was then calculated as the ratio of SPY to FNPP. Trait evaluation and scoring procedures followed the guidelines of the International Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants (UPOV) for tomato [ 22 ]. Sunscald incidence was evaluated as the percentage of sunscald-affected fruits among 100 randomly harvested fruits per genotype, whereas persistent calyx in fruits (PCF) was recorded as the percentage of fruits retaining the calyx at harvest. For fruit quality and morphological traits, sampling was performed to minimize positional effects by collecting fruits from plants located in the central area of each plot. At the red-ripe stage (full physiological maturity), five representative fruits per genotype were harvested and transferred to the laboratory for detailed measurements. Fruit length (FL, mm), fruit width (FW, mm), and pericarp thickness (PTH, mm) were measured using digital calipers. The number of locules was determined as the mean of five fruits per genotype. Fruit firmness was evaluated using a manual sensory assessment. Five ripe fruits per genotype were assessed by multiple trained evaluators through gentle hand pressure and scored on an ordinal scale (1 = soft, 2 = intermediate, 3 = firm). Fruit juice pH was measured using a calibrated digital pH meter. Titratable acidity (TA) was determined by titrating 10 mL of freshly extracted juice, diluted to 100 mL with distilled water, using 0.1 N NaOH to an endpoint of pH 8.2. Titratable acidity was expressed as grams of citric acid equivalent per 100 mL of juice [ 23 ]. Total soluble solids content was measured as °Brix using a digital refractometer. Fruit shelf life (SHL) was evaluated using five healthy fruits per genotype stored at 25 °C in a well-ventilated room under ambient conditions and protected from direct sunlight. Fruit condition was monitored daily, and the number of days until visible deterioration or loss of marketable quality was recorded as the shelf-life index.
Data were analyzed using analysis of variance (ANOVA) based on an augmented randomized complete block design. For traits evaluated across check cultivars, mean comparisons were conducted using Duncan’s Multiple Range Test (DMRT) at the 5% probability level. To account for block effects and improve genotype comparisons, data were analyzed using ANOVA with control-based adjustments. Continuous quantitative traits were assessed using standard ANOVA procedures after verifying model assumptions (e.g., residual normality), while non-parametric traits, including count and ordinal data, were analyzed using the Kruskal–Wallis test.

All statistical analyses were performed separately for each trait (TYLCV resistance, NIMS, NFI, and NFPI) using R software (v4.4.2) with the packages dplyr , readxl , and writexl .
Analysis of variance conducted on the control cultivars revealed that block effects were not statistically significant for any of the evaluated traits, including TYLCV severity. Therefore, no block-based correction was required for the performance of parental lines or hybrids across blocks, indicating uniform natural infection pressure for TYLCV throughout the experimental field. The block effects for the other evaluated traits were non-significant as well. Disease severity scores among genotypes ranged from 0 to 5, with an overall mean of 1.088, confirming that the level of infection pressure was sufficient to reliably discriminate between resistant and susceptible responses. The susceptible control cultivar ‘Matin’ exhibited the highest mean disease severity score (2.764), confirming its effectiveness as a spreader genotype and ensuring homogeneous virus distribution under field conditions. In contrast, the remaining genotypes showed greater resistance and contributed less to overall TYLCV incidence (Fig. 1 ). The contrasting responses of tomato genotypes to TYLCV infection are illustrated in Fig. 2 , where the severe disease symptoms observed in the susceptible cultivar ‘Matin’ are compared with the symptom-free resistant hybrids.

A comprehensive summary of the mean heterosis values for these traits is presented in Table 1 . The distribution patterns and variability of MPH and BPH across all traits are illustrated using boxplots in Figs. 3 and 4 , respectively. Additionally, dot plots depicting the statistical significance of each hybrid–trait combination are provided in Supplementary Figs. S1 and S2.

Trait abbreviations are as follows: SPY – single-plant yield; SFW – single fruit weight; FNPP – fruit number per plant; FL – fruit length; FW – fruit width; PTH – pericarp thickness; NIMS– number of inflorescences on the main stem; NFI–number of flowers per inflorescence; NFPI–number of fruits per inflorescence; SHL – shelf life; Firmness – fruit firmness; PCF– percentage of persistent calyx in fruits; Locules – number of locules per fruit; Sunscald– percentage of sunscald-affected fruits; pH – fruit acidity; TA – titratable acidity; Brix – total soluble solids; TYLCV – Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus resistance
The heterosis analysis revealed two distinct categories of traits: (i) those for which positive heterosis values are desirable (e.g., yield, fruit number, and fruit size–related traits), and (ii) those where negative heterosis indicates improvement (e.g., sunscald incidence, TYLCV resistance, and fruit acidity–related trait). Within the first category, the highest levels of positive heterosis were observed for SPY, with a mean MPH of 40.10% and more than 90% of hybrids displaying positive MPH. Similarly, FNPP and FW showed consistently high positive heterosis values, underscoring the strong potential of hybridization for yield enhancement. In the second category, where negative heterosis was favorable, notable patterns emerged. For sunscald incidence, mean heterosis values were − 25.05% (MPH) and − 50.06% (BPH). Strikingly, over two-thirds of the hybrids (68.6% for MPH and 76.5% for BPH) showed significant reductions in sunscald, highlighting the potential of hybrid combinations to improve fruit quality under light-stress conditions. TYLCV resistance, a key trait in this study, exhibited a wide heterosis range (− 100% to + 620% for MPH). Although the mean heterosis was modestly positive for MPH (8.71%) and negative for BPH (− 24.49%), more than half of the hybrids (52.95% for MPH and 56.87% for BPH) displayed negative heterosis, indicating enhanced resistance compared with both parents. Notably, 24 hybrids exhibited − 100% heterosis, representing a valuable outcome from a breeding perspective. For internal fruit quality attribute, negative heterosis was also advantageous. Fruit pH displayed high frequencies of negative heterosis: 54.9% of hybrids for MPH, and 80.4% for BPH. These results suggest that hybridization can effectively improve flavor quality and achieve a more balanced acidity profile in tomato fruits. Interestingly, although traits such as NFI and NFPI exhibited predominantly negative heterosis in our study, this pattern aligns with the theoretical framework proposed by Krieger et al. [ 5 ], who showed that yield heterosis in tomato is largely driven by an increase in NIMS rather than enhanced productivity within individual inflorescences. Consistent with this model, we observed strong positive heterosis for SPY and FNPP, indicating that reproductive unit proliferation is the main contributor to yield improvement. For example, hybrids from ♂73 × ♀50 and ♂73 × ♀151 produced four inflorescences versus two in their parents, while hybrids from ♂323 × ♀332 and ♂323 × ♀290 produced five versus three, clearly demonstrating heterotic effects. These findings support the dosage-dependent mechanism described by Krieger et al. [ 5 ], whereby heterozygosity fine-tunes the balance between vegetative and reproductive growth, ultimately enhancing floral productivity. A representative comparison of fruit morphology between the parental inbred lines and their selected superior F₁ hybrids is shown in Fig. 5 , highlighting the phenotypic differences associated with hybrid vigor.

These hybrids were identified as superior based on heterosis analysis across multiple traits, and their parental lines exhibited favorable GCA for reproductive traits and TYLCV resistance, making them recommended candidates for broader breeding programs

The analysis of variance based on the North Carolina II (NCII) crossing design revealed differential and statistically significant contributions of male (m), female (f), and their interaction (m × f) effects to the variation observed in floral and virus resistance traits (Table 2 ). For NIMS and NFI, both male and female effects were significant ( p < 0.05), whereas the male × female interaction was non-significant, indicating that additive genetic effects predominantly control these traits. This suggests that selecting superior parents with strong GCA is more effective than relying on specific hybrid combinations. Interestingly, for NFPI, although both parental effects were significant, the absence of interaction again underscored the predominance of additive variance, with a stronger contribution from male parents. These findings are consistent with the model of Krieger et al. [ 5 ], which proposed that tomato yield heterosis is primarily driven by increased inflorescence number rather than per-inflorescence productivity. In contrast, TYLCV resistance exhibited highly significant male, female, and interaction effects ( p < 0.01), highlighting the involvement of both additive and non-additive gene actions. The significant interaction term reflects the importance of SCA and possible epistasis, suggesting that hybrid breeding is essential to achieve durable resistance. Therefore, both careful parental selection and targeted hybrid development are essential for improving TYLCV resistance.

The variance component analysis (Table 3 ) revealed contrasting genetic architectures across traits. For NIMS and NFI, additive variance slightly exceeded non-additive variance, with dominance degrees (1.26 and 1.19) indicating partial to full overdominance. Both h² and H² were high, suggesting that selection of elite parents with strong GCA, combined with hybrid breeding, can efficiently improve these traits. For NFPI, additive variance was much higher than non-additive variance, with D < 1 (0.58), consistent with incomplete dominance and strong additive control. This indicates that direct selection in early generations and recurrent selection in later cycles are effective strategies. Notably, for TYLCV resistance, the non-additive variance (4.11) was much greater than the additive component (0.94), with a high dominance degree (2.95), reflecting a pattern of strong overdominance. Despite a moderate h N ² of 0.43, the high H B ² value of 0.99 indicates that genetic factors account for most of the phenotypic variance (Fig. 6 ). These findings underscore the importance of non-additive gene action and epistasis, suggesting that hybrid breeding and heterosis exploitation are the most efficient approaches for improving resistance to TYLCV. These results align with the model of Krieger et al. [ 5 ], in which yield heterosis in tomato is largely explained by dosage-dependent effects on reproductive proliferation. Similarly, the predominance of additive variance for inflorescence traits supports the idea that heterozygosity at key loci enhances reproductive unit number, while the strong non-additive control of TYLCV resistance emphasizes the strategic value of exploiting SCA in hybrid development under biotic stress.

To further dissect the genetic basis of key reproductive and virus-resistance traits, general combining ability (GCA) was estimated for four traits: NFI, NFPI, NIMS, and severity of TYLCV infection across male and female parents (Figs. 7 and 8 ). Male parents 323, 73, and 79, together with female lines 50, 332, 164, and 151, consistently exhibited favorable GCA effects for multiple reproductive traits. Notably, these high-GCA parents were also involved in hybrids showing pronounced heterosis, indicating a strong concordance between combining ability and heterotic performance. For TYLCV resistance, negative GCA effects are desirable as they indicate reduced disease severity. Female line 50 showed the most negative GCA value, while male parents 323 and 73, along with female lines 332, 140, and 151, also demonstrated significant negative GCA. These genotypes represent valuable resources for breeding virus-resistant hybrids. Importantly, the alignment between GCA estimates and heterotic outcomes supports the dosage-dependent mechanism proposed by Krieger et al. [ 5 ], in which heterozygosity fine-tunes the balance between vegetative growth and reproductive allocation. The identified parents, therefore, represent promising candidates for multi-trait hybrid breeding, combining high reproductive potential with durable virus resistance.

Specific combining ability (SCA) was analyzed to capture non-additive genetic effects and identify high-performing parental combinations for four key traits: NFI, NFPI, NIMS, and TYLCV severity (Fig. 9 ). Heatmaps of SCA values revealed substantial variation in parental interactions across traits, underscoring the critical role of non-additive effects in tomato hybrid performance. For TYLCV resistance, negative SCA values were favorable, and several hybrid combinations (451 × 176, 150 × 151, and 150 × 548) exhibited highly negative SCA, highlighting their potential as virus-resistant hybrids. For NFPI, which reflects successful fruit set, crosses such as 554 × 598, 150 × 240, and 323 × 151 showed superior SCA, suggesting enhanced reproductive efficiency. Similarly, for NFI, hybrids 323 × 151, 150 × 240, 554 × 164, and 554 × 420 displayed positive SCA, indicating strong flowering capacity. In the case of NIMS, combinations such as 323 × 176, 554 × 52, and 554 × 151 showed high positive SCA, reflecting enhanced inflorescence production. Overall, hybrids exhibiting favorable SCA across multiple traits represent multi-trait candidates for targeted breeding programs. Importantly, the strong SCA effects for TYLCV resistance reinforce the role of epistasis and overdominance, consistent with the theoretical framework proposed by Krieger et al. [ 5 ]. This suggests that heterozygosity at key loci not only enhances reproductive growth but also contributes to improved stress tolerance and TYLCV resistance by balancing resource allocation between yield and defense. Comprehensive SCA values for all crosses are presented in Fig. 10 for comparative reference.

To explore the genetic relationships among reproductive and resistance traits at the level of non-additive effects, Spearman’s correlation analysis was conducted using SCA values for NFI, NFPI, NIMS, and TYLCV severity. The resulting heatmap (Fig. 11 a) revealed a strong positive and significant correlation between NFI and NFPI ( r = 0.55), indicating genetic alignment between flowering capacity and fruit set efficiency in hybrids. Weaker, non-significant positive correlations were also detected between NIMS and other reproductive traits (e.g., NIMS vs. NFPI, r = 0.14), suggesting that inflorescence structure may modestly influence yield potential. In contrast, TYLCV resistance showed negative and non-significant correlations with reproductive traits (e.g., NFPI, r = − 0.12), pointing to genetic independence between resistance mechanisms and yield-related attributes. This independence is advantageous for breeding programs, as it allows simultaneous improvement of yield and resistance without genetic conflict, and is consistent with the model of Krieger et al. [ 5 ], where heterosis is driven mainly by reproductive proliferation rather than stress-related traits. In addition, correlations between mean GCA and SCA effects were assessed to examine their interdependence (Fig. 11 b). Across all traits, correlations were low and statistically non-significant, with the highest observed in NFPI ( r = 0.12) and the lowest in NFI ( r = − 0.04). These findings highlight that GCA does not reliably predict SCA, underscoring the necessity of jointly considering both components when selecting parents and designing crosses.

To evaluate the contribution of non-additive effects to phenotypic expression, scatter plots were generated between SCA estimates and observed values for NFI, NFPI, NIMS, and TYLCV severity (Fig. 12 ). For reproductive traits, clear positive trends were observed, indicating that hybrids with higher SCA values generally achieved superior phenotypic performance. This confirms the critical role of dominance and epistasis in enhancing flowering and fruit-setting traits. For TYLCV, the relationship was inverse: hybrids with more negative SCA values tended to exhibit lower infection severity, consistent with the role of non-additive variance in conferring resistance. Although the association was weaker than for reproductive traits, the overall trend highlights the value of SCA as a predictive tool for identifying both high-yielding and TYLCV-resistant hybrids.

Only hybrid combinations with significant positive SCA for NIMS, NFI, and NFPI, and significant negative SCA for TYLCV resistance were included to reflect enhanced performance or improved virus resistance, respectively (Fig. 13 ).

The TYLCV resistance network revealed that a subset of male and female parents consistently contributed to resistant hybrids, underscoring the importance of specific parental genotypes in conferring virus resistance through non-additive interactions. In contrast, for NIMS and NFI, certain parents were repeatedly associated with positive SCA effects, highlighting favorable additive × dominance interactions that promote inflorescence initiation and flowering. The NFPI network displayed a more balanced contribution from both parental groups, indicating complementary gene action in fruit set. These findings complement the ANOVA and variance component analyses, confirming that while additive effects shape baseline performance, non-additive interactions largely determine hybrid superiority. From a theoretical perspective, the recurrent appearance of certain high-contributing parents is consistent with the dosage-dependent mechanism proposed by Krieger et al. [ 5 ], where heterozygosity fine-tunes the balance between vegetative and reproductive growth. Overall, these network analyses provide a clear graphical overview of SCA patterns and highlight parental combinations most influential for trait improvement, thereby offering a practical decision-making tool for designing future hybrid breeding programs. Detailed SCA network data for all traits are provided in Supplementary Tables S1–S4.
The NCII-based analysis of variance in this study revealed that the patterns of genetic control varied across the evaluated traits. Flowering traits, including NIMS, NFI, and NFPI, were predominantly governed by additive genetic effects, as indicated by significant male and female parental effects and the absence of significant male × female interactions. In contrast, TYLCV resistance exhibited significant effects of both parents and their interaction, indicating the involvement of both additive and non-additive genetic components, including SCA. These findings suggest that while selection of superior parents is effective for improving flowering traits, hybrid development is essential for enhancing TYLCV resistance, which is consistent with previous reports [ 25 , 26 ].
Genetic variance estimates further highlighted these differences. TYLCV resistance displayed strong overdominance (D = 2.95) and very high broad-sense heritability (H² = 0.99), reflecting a decisive role for non-additive effects (σ²_SCA = 4.11). These results confirm the critical role of dominance and epistatic interactions in conferring resistance and support the application of hybrid breeding and parent selection based on SCA [ 27 – 29 ]. Reproductive traits NIMS and NFI showed a moderate degree of dominance with substantial additive contributions, confirming that hybrid breeding strategies should balance parental selection and heterosis exploitation [ 30 ]. In contrast, NFPI exhibited low dominance (D = 0.58) and the lowest broad-sense heritability (H²B = 0.67), indicating primarily additive control and higher environmental sensitivity, thus favoring direct selection in later generations [ 31 ]. This partitioning of genetic control aligns with the dosage-dependent model of Krieger et al. [ 5 ], which proposed that heterosis for yield arises largely from additive effects that increase the number of reproductive units, whereas resistance and stress tolerance rely more on non-additive interactions.
Both GCA and SCA were important for the studied traits (NFI, NFPI, NIMS, and TYLCV resistance), but their relative contributions differed, consistent with previous reports [ 2 , 28 ]. GCA were particularly prominent for total yield and vegetative traits, ensuring trait stability across generations [ 28 ], whereas SCA effects predominated in several traits, especially those associated with fruit set and early yield, underscoring the importance of exploiting heterosis [ 29 , 32 ]. These findings are in line with the present results and indicate that selecting parents solely based on high GCA without considering SCA does not guarantee superior hybrids. The predominance of non-additive genetic variance and high SCA for TYLCV resistance observed in this study indicates that resistance expression is strongly dependent on specific parental combinations. Although molecular markers were not used to identify specific resistance genes in the present study, the lack of association between yield components and TYLCV resistance suggests that the resistance observed in selected hybrids is independent of yield. These patterns are consistent with previous reports showing that major TYLCV resistance genes such as Ty-1 and Ty-3 confer virus resistance without yield penalties [ 33 , 34 ]. These findings support the effectiveness of hybrid breeding strategies for improving TYLCV resistance without compromising yield performance.
The integration of GCA and SCA results provided further insights. For example, strong positive heterosis for SPY and FNPP was observed in crosses where both parents had contrasting growth habits, consistent with the framework proposed by Krieger et al. [ 5 ]. This reflects the idea that heterozygosity fine-tunes the balance between vegetative and reproductive growth, leading to higher yield potential. In contrast, TYLCV resistance was maximized in crosses where non-additive effects predominated, confirming that defense-related traits benefit more from hybrid-specific genetic interactions than from additive parental contributions.
The Spearman correlation analysis between mean GCA and SCA values for reproductive traits and TYLCV resistance showed very weak and non-significant associations. This indicates that relying solely on GCA to predict hybrid performance is insufficient, a finding consistent with Liu et al. [ 2 ], who reported no significant GCA–SCA correlation across eight tomato traits, and with Su et al. [ 35 ], who emphasized the lack of continuity between these components. Moreover, line × tester analyses have indicated that high SCA combinations do not necessarily originate from high-GCA parents, but often from those with low to medium GCA [ 36 ]. Therefore, simultaneous evaluation of both GCA and SCA is essential for parent selection and precise breeding design.
This study also revealed a relatively strong positive and significant correlation ( r = 0.55) between NFI and NFPI, suggesting that increased reproductive capacity of the inflorescence can effectively enhance fruit set. This finding is consistent with Wijaya et al. [ 37 ], who reported in Jatropha curcas that inflorescence structure was a key determinant of fruit production. Moreover, no negative correlation was detected between TYLCV resistance and reproductive traits, indicating that simultaneous breeding for high yield and TYLCV resistance is feasible [ 33 , 34 ]. Identification of genotypes with high flowering and fruiting capacity, especially under heat and drought stress, may substantially improve yield potential [ 38 ].
Our findings are consistent with previous reports indicating that, in tomato, dominance for fruit size traits often favors small-fruit alleles. For instance, the small-fruit allele fw2.2 acts in a dominant or semi-dominant manner, significantly reducing fruit weight even in the presence of large-fruit alleles [ 39 , 40 ]. On the other hand, recent studies have demonstrated that this pattern can be more complex; for example, the large-fruit allele of fw6.3 exhibits overdominance, producing F1 fruits heavier than both parents [ 41 ], whereas the small-fruit allele of fw3.3 sometimes shows a reversed effect, even contributing to increased fruit weight [ 42 ]. Moreover, recent GWAS analyses have confirmed the existence of diverse dominance patterns among QTLs controlling fruit weight [ 43 ]. In line with this evidence, our data also showed positive mean heterosis for FNPP, while BPH for SFW was negative. This pattern likely reflects a source–sink trade-off, where an increase in fruit number per plant is generally accompanied by a reduction in individual fruit weight. Overall, these results indicate that both the genetic dominance of small-fruit alleles and physiological constraints in resource allocation play key roles in shaping the observed heterosis patterns.
Finally, several superior hybrids were identified that combined high yield potential with TYLCV resistance. Some of these exhibited complete resistance and strong positive heterosis for SPY, providing practical evidence that the dosage-dependent model of Krieger et al. [ 5 ] can be extended beyond controlled experiments to field-based breeding programs. Our results are consistent with recent reports highlighting the predominant role of non-additive effects and the feasibility of simultaneously enhancing yield and resistance [ 2 , 32 , 33 ]. Together, these findings highlight a dual breeding strategy: (i) emphasize additive effects and parental selection for reproductive and yield traits, and (ii) exploit non-additive interactions through hybridization for TYLCV resistance and stress adaptation. This approach aligns with global trends that classify traits according to inheritance patterns (additive or non-additive) and adjust breeding strategies accordingly [ 2 , 44 , 45 ].
This study provides comprehensive insights into the genetic architecture of floral traits and TYLCV resistance in tomato using NCII-based analysis. Additive gene action predominated in traits such as NIMS, NFI, and NFPI, indicating that selection of superior parental lines can effectively enhance reproductive potential. In contrast, TYLCV resistance was largely governed by non-additive effects, emphasizing the need for strategic hybrid development and the exploitation of specific combining ability to achieve durable resistance. Notably, several hybrids (e.g., 323 × 332, 323 × 50, and 73 × 332) combined strong SCA for yield traits with complete viral resistance despite low parental GCA, highlighting the genetic independence of resistance from productivity. This independence provides opportunities for the simultaneous improvement of yield and resilience. Moreover, the lack of significant correlations between GCA and SCA, and between TYLCV resistance and yield traits, reinforces the necessity of integrating both genetic components in hybrid prediction. Collectively, these findings support a dual breeding strategy: leveraging additive effects for reproductive traits while exploiting heterosis and molecular tools such as marker-assisted and genomic selection to develop high-yielding, virus-resistant tomato cultivars.

title: DeepTYLCV: An interpretable and experimentally validated AI model for predicting virulence of different tomato yellow leaf curl virus strains
text:

Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) is among the most devastating pathogens affecting tomato production worldwide, with emerging virulent strains increasingly overcoming genetic resistance and triggering severe outbreaks. Traditional field diagnosis, reliant on visual inspection or image-based AI models, remains constrained by symptom dependence, environmental variability, and poor strain-level interpretability. To address these challenges, we introduce DeepTYLCV, a novel deep learning framework for accurate virulence prediction directly from viral-genome-derived open reading frame sequences. We first constructed a comprehensive dataset of globally sourced TYLCV sequences curated by virulence annotations. DeepTYLCV integrates protein language model-based embeddings with optimal concatenated conventional descriptors using a hybrid architecture composed of a transformer encoder and a multi-scale convolutional neural network, enabling effective extraction of both global and local sequence features. Benchmark analyses demonstrate that DeepTYLCV significantly outperforms our previously developed IML-TYLCV model, which was trained on Korean isolates and lacked global generalizability. Importantly, blind predictions on 15 uncharacterized or representative TYLCV isolates were experimentally validated in tomato plants, achieving 100% concordance between model predictions and observed symptom severity. Furthermore, 1D-Grad-CAM++-based interpretability analyses revealed that the model consistently focused on relevant sequence motifs associated with severe strains, offering mechanistic insights into symptom severity. DeepTYLCV is publicly available at https://balalab-skku.org/DeepTYLCV/ and represents a powerful, interpretable, and globally scalable platform for early TYLCV surveillance, resistance monitoring, and strategic disease management in tomato cultivation.
This study introduces DeepTYLCV, a deep learning framework for predicting the virulence of tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV) directly from viral ORF sequences. The model integrates protein language model embeddings in a hybrid Transformer–MSCNN architecture and outperforms the previous IML-TYLCV model in global prediction tasks. DeepTYLCV predictions were further validated experimentally on 15 viral isolates, achieving 100% concordance. These results highlight the potential of DeepTYLCV as an accurate, interpretable, and scalable tool for TYLCV surveillance and disease management.
